---
title: "Metagame, Time Use, and Player Development in Online Chess: A Large-Scale Study of Lichess Games"
author: "Camden Bergquist"
date: "Last compiled on `r format(Sys.time(), '%B %d, %Y')`"
abstract: >
  Metagame change, time management, and player development are central but often separately studied dimensions of online chess behavior. Using 24 months of public Lichess data from January 2024 through December 2025, this study builds a reproducible large-scale pipeline that samples rated games and derives linked datasets for metagame composition, opening repertoire, time use, and longitudinal player outcomes. The analysis is observational and non-causal, and combines descriptive modeling, multinomial opening models, player fixed-effects progression models, and clustering-based behavioral profiling with forward-in-time evaluation. The results indicate that the opening environment gradually spreads across a wider set of choices over time, although the extent of that spread differs by time control. Opening preferences also shift with skill, as stronger players devote a smaller share of games to the most common named openings. Patterns of time use vary by format: Higher-rated players move faster in blitz, think longer in rapid and classical, and enter low-time situations more often across all formats. In models of within-player change, later rating gains are linked more consistently to richer and less-static opening repertoires and to more complex games than to sheer game volume. Clustering results likewise suggest that chess behavior is better understood as a set of recurring play states than as a small number of fixed player types. These findings suggest that improvement in online chess is tied less to sheer volume of play than to how players allocate attention, manage time pressure, and vary their strategic choices. More broadly, the results show how large-scale game logs can be used to study adaptation and skill development in online-chess environments.

## Introduction

Competitive games have become an important source of large-scale behavioral data, enabling researchers to study strategic decision-making, skill development, and population-level trends using observational logs at scales rarely achievable in controlled studies [@edelmann2020css; @watts2014css]. Chess is one of the most-played competitive games in the world, and the relatively recent growth of online platforms has created datasets with millions to billions of games played under standardized rules and well-defined competitive contexts (e.g., time controls, ratings, game outcomes, etc.) [@watts2014css; @lichessDatabase]. One of the most widely used sources is the Lichess Open Database, which provides public monthly exports of rated games played on lichess.org in PGN format [@lichessDatabase; @lichessDatabaseGitHub]. These exports make it possible to study the ways strategy and performance vary across skill levels and time controls in a modern, online environment.

This study uses Lichess game data to investigate contemporary metagame behavior and player development. Here, 'metagame' refers to the population-level distribution of strategic choices and styles observed in practice – such as opening families, risk preferences, and game outcomes – within a defined time window and player population. In addition to describing how strategic behavior differs by rating and time control, we attempt to connect these strategic signatures to measures of player progression over time. Because online chess is a repeatedly played competitive setting with a mature rating infrastructure, it offers a natural testbed for quantifying skill and comparing behavior across a large player population [@lichessRatingSystems; @glickmanGlicko2Desc].

A central component of modern chess analytics is the rating system used to summarize player strength. The ELO rating system – a system originally developed for chess – models player performance probabilistically, and remains a foundational reference point for interpreting skill differences and expected outcomes in competitive settings [@elo1978rating; @fideElo2025]. Lichess uses a modified version of this system called 'Glicko-2', which, in addition to rating, tracks uncertainty via rating deviation and volatility [@lichessRatingSystems; @glickmanGlicko2Desc]. Skill ratings are especially useful for observational studies like this one because they provide a consistent scale by which to stratify players and construct longitudinal measures of improvement [@glickmanGlicko2Desc].

Overall, this project brings together data science, computational social science, and strategic-behavior research by treating online chess as a real-world environment in which strategic choices and performance outcomes can be measured at scale and analyzed using statistical learning methods [@edelmann2020css; @watts2014css].

### Background {#sec-background}

A growing research literature uses large online chess datasets to study human performance, decision-making, and strategic patterns. For example, Chowdhary et al. use an online chess dataset of more than 100 million games to quantify performance dynamics and career-like trajectories, illustrating how large game archives support population-level behavioral measurement across skill levels [@chowdhary2023performance].

One important line of work focuses on time usage and decision quality under time constraints. Online chess platforms record both move sequences and clock information, which allows researchers to study how players allocate thinking time and how time pressure shapes decisions. Russek et al. analyze millions of Lichess games to relate move times to the estimated value of additional computation, and show that time allocation patterns vary systematically with playing strength and time control [@russek2025thinking]. These findings support the idea that online chess is a rich setting for studying bounded rationality and performance under constraints, especially when comparing bullet, blitz, rapid, and classical formats [@russek2025thinking].

Chess opening choice is also an active research topic. Because openings are discrete, labelable strategic choices that occur early in every game, they are well suited to population-level analysis. De Marzo and Servedio use online chess community data to quantify opening similarity and complexity, including representing openings in network form and studying how opening-related structure can be used to forecast future opening adoption [@demarzo2023openings]. This motivates analyzing metagame development in terms of shifting opening popularity and success rates across time, player skill, and time controls [@demarzo2023openings; @chowdhary2023performance].

Finally, there is an emerging interest in identifying player styles or archetypes from game logs. While traditional chess analysis often focuses on engine evaluation of positions, a complementary approach is to extract behavioral features from move sequences and outcomes (e.g., game length, opening selection, and other style proxies) and use statistical learning to characterize player types. For instance, McIlroy-Young et al. demonstrate that models trained on move sequences can capture individual-specific signatures ('style') in player decisions, supporting the notion that player behavior is meaningfully distinguishable from game records alone [@mcilroyyoung2021stylometry]. This creates a bridge between strategic analysis (what players choose to do) and longitudinal outcomes (how players improve or persist over time).

Collectively, existing work suggests that large-scale online chess datasets support three relevant kinds of analysis: (1) descriptive metagame analysis of strategic choices across populations; (2) modeling the way constraints (such as time pressure) affect behavior and outcomes; and (3) data-driven modeling of player growth and characterization of potential player types [@chowdhary2023performance; @russek2025thinking; @demarzo2023openings; @mcilroyyoung2021stylometry]. Here, we build on those themes by using Lichess data to analyze contemporary opening and style patterns and relate them to measures of player performance and development over time.

## The Data {#sec-data}

### Source {#sec-source}
<!--
Describe where this data comes from, why it was collected, who collected it, and how it was collected. A Citation may be useful here.
-->
Lichess is the largest open-source chess server in the world and releases free monthly exports of its game data under the Creative Commons CC0 license [@lichessDatabase]. The site logs game data while a game is being played, and allows users to retroactively analyze both the games they've played and those of others on the platform. Although Lichess offers a powerful API, we elected to download data directly from their website in `.pgn.zst` format. The PGN (portable game notation) format is a plaintext format for chess games, containing moves, metadata headers (e.g., players, date, and event), and optional annotation. The `.zst` file extension denotes Zstandard compression, a modern compression format commonly used for its speed and efficiency. In practice, Zstandard substantially reduces the storage required for large PGN archives.

For the purposes of this study, we downloaded 24 months of Lichess game data spanning from January 2024 to December 2025, amounting to ~677 gigabytes of raw data when compressed. Nearly 700 gigabytes of compressed data – roughly 3–4 terabytes uncompressed – was too large to process conveniently on local hardware alone. We therefore relied on a hybrid R/Python pipeline that downloads the data, deterministically samples and parses it into partitioned parquet files, and then constructs smaller analysis-ready datasets from those outputs.

The download and parsing section of the pipeline performs the following:

- Reads a config file `pipeline.yml` that controls the scope and parameters of the pipeline's operation.
- Downloads monthly Lichess 'standard rated' PGN archives for each month specified in the YAML.
- Decompresses each Zstandard file as a stream, scanning games one-by-one to prevent memory bottlenecks.
- Parses game headers first to determine whether a game meets the sampling and filtering criteria before doing more expensive parsing work.
  - Extracts core metadata (players, ratings, time control, result, termination, opening, timestamps).
  - Buckets each game into blitz/rapid/classical using the Lichess time-control convention.
- Applies filtering rules from the YAML, which in this case are:
  - Only include blitz/rapid/classical time controls.
  - Only include games from players in the 800–2600 rating range.
  - Drops unwanted terminations (aborted games).
- Uses deterministic hash-based sampling to create reproducible subsets without needing to store the whole population:
  - A meta sample keyed by `game_id` for population/metagame summaries, at a rate of 5/500 games.
  - A player cohort keyed by `username` for longitudinal/player tracking at a rate of 3/500 players.
  - A moves sample keyed by `game_id` for clock/time-per-move data at a rate of 5/10000 moves.
- Deterministically anonymizes usernames based on a stable, salted hash.
  - Cohort selection is computed on the real username before anonymization, so it remains reproducible.
- Writes month-partitioned parquet outputs for game-level data.

The dataset-building portion of the pipeline takes those outputs and, using DuckDB to read and write parquet files on the disk, builds seven datasets from them:

- Player-level longitudinal summary tables from `games_cohort`:
  - `player_month` (`pm`): $\text{player} \times \text{month}$, 249,761 observations.
  - `player_month_tc` (`pm_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 320,869 observations.
- Player-opening 'repertoire' table from `games_cohort`:
  - `player_opening_month_tc` (`pom_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control} \times \text{opening}$, 7,167,580 observations.
- Metagame tables from `games_meta`:
  - `meta_opening_month_tc` (`mom_tc`): $\text{openings} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 130,672 observations.
  - `meta_month_tc` (`mm_tc`): $\text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 72 observations.
- Time-usage tables from `moves_meta`:
  - `player_time_month_tc` (`ptm_tc`): $\text{player} \times \text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 1,038,050 observations.
  - `moves_month_tc` (`mvm_tc`) $\text{month} \times \text{time control}$, 72 observations.

The pipeline logs session and version info for both R and Python and records checksums for downloaded raw files to help with reproducibility.

### Variables

The analysis uses several linked derived datasets rather than a single analytic table. In all cases, the raw unit of data is a rated chess game from the Lichess public database, but the pipeline aggregates games and sometimes moves into analysis-ready summaries. At the player level, `pm` and `pm_tc` summarize monthly outcomes overall and by time control; `pom_tc` captures opening use within player-month-time-control cells; `ptm_tc` summarizes move-time behavior; and `mom_tc` and `mm_tc` provide population-level metagame summaries. Because these tables operate at different units of analysis, the main text introduces them only at the level needed for later modeling. Full variable definitions are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-a].

Together, these analytical levels support longitudinal player-performance modeling (`pm`, `pm_tc`), repertoire and style measurement from opening choice (`pom_tc`), metagame analysis via opening adoption and outcomes (`mom_tc`), and time-management analysis using move-time features (`ptm_tc`).^[The remaining tables `mm_tc` and `mvm_tc` are summary-level datasets that aren't explicitly modeled.]

### Cleaning

Most cleaning steps were performed during the pipeline’s parsing stage. Additional standardization and feature construction steps not covered in @sec-source include:

- `TimeControl` tag parsed into:
  - `initial` (seconds).
  - `increment` (seconds).
  - `tc_bucket` (< 180 = bullet, < 600 = blitz, < 1800 = rapid, else classical),
- Converted PGN result strings into:
  - `winner` (white/black/draw).
  - `score_white` (1/0.5/0).
- Computed upset indicators using ratings:
  - `rating_diff` = `white_rating` - `black_rating`.
  - `abs_rating_diff`
  - `is_upset`
- Computed game length in `moves` from move sequences for use in the derived datasets.

The resulting data were then restructured and aggregated into tidy analysis tables.

## Exploratory Data Analysis {#sec-eda}

This section summarizes the main descriptive patterns in the sampled data before formal modeling. It first documents support and reliability constraints that affect interpretation, then turns to broad patterns in opening behavior and time usage. Full supporting diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b].

### Coverage and Reliability{#sec-eda-coverage}

Before turning to observed patterns, it is useful to clarify which parts of the sampled data are more and less strongly supported. @fig-coverage shows that the number of observations differs substantially across time controls, with blitz appearing more often than rapid, and both appearing much more often than classical. This is a direct consequence of our parsing method: The pipeline sampled from the underlying game population rather than enforcing balanced coverage by format. As such, the cleaned data preserve the activity structure of the platform itself. That is not a problem in its own right, but it does mean that comparisons across time controls come with unequal precision, especially where classical is concerned.

<!--
@fig-coverage, the first and most important of the EDA plots, shows the number of observations the parser sampled per player-month, colored by time control.^[Throughout, 'rows' refer to aggregated observation units (e.g., player-month-time-control or opening-month-time-control records), whereas 'games' refer to the underlying sampled matches contributing to those aggregates. A change in row counts therefore reflects changes in the breadth of observed groups, not necessarily a change in total game volume.] It highlights a fundamental flaw in my parsing method— one that I failed to consider until seeing it visualized. See, while the parser filters the raw data down to a smaller subset of time controls and rating ranges, it does nothing to ensure that there's an equal distribution of games for given time controls or players of given ratings. Rather, it simply samples in a pseudo-random manner. This means that the distribution of certain variables in the cleaned dataset will reflect the true distribution of those variables among all games stored in the Lichess database. In more straightforward terms, popular time controls like blitz are played more often than less-popular ones like classical, and that relationship is mirrored in the data, as evidenced in @fig-coverage.

This finding isn't the end of the world, but it *is* extremely important to control for. It means that some 'missingness' will be structural rather than truly random, and that there will be a general imbalance across time controls, ratings, and months. It also justifies restricting certain analyses to blitz/rapid (or else collapsing them entirely), adding minimum-support thresholds to ensure there's enough data, and treating month as a potential confound only when coverage is stable enough; buckets with adequate support will be emphasized, and low-support buckets should be treated as exploratory only.
-->

```{r Coverage Plot}
#| label: fig-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of observations per time control is skewed due to the sampling method used when parsing. Any estimate that compares time controls will have unequal precision, especially where classical is concerned. "
#| fig-align: center

cov_pm_tc <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT month, tc_bucket, COUNT(*) AS n_rows
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY month, tc_bucket
  ORDER BY month, tc_bucket
", qpath(paths$pm_tc)))

ggplot(cov_pm_tc, aes(x = month, y = n_rows, group = tc_bucket, color = tc_bucket)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Observations", title = "Coverage of PM_TC Table", color = "Time Control") +
  scale_color_few(labels = c("Blitz", "Classical", "Rapid")) +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```
<!--
@fig-reliability and @fig-panel-depth display two different kinds of unreliability inherent to player-month: the former being the number of games played in a given month, and the latter the number of months each player is present for in the data (total; not necessarily consecutive). For @fig-reliability, many player-months contain few games, making outcomes like win rate or average rating noisy at the unit level, justifying a minimum-games filter for player-month analyses, weighting player-month observations by games in aggregated models, and preferring aggregated measures such as bins over raw point clouds; game count should be treated as a precision/weighting signal.
-->

A second limitation is that the player panel is unbalanced. @fig-panel-depth shows that many players appear for only a few months, while a much smaller subset remain observable across all or most of the two-year window. That's about what one should expect from an online hobby setting, but it matters once the analysis shifts from cross-sectional summaries to player-level change over time. Any lagged or forward-looking quantity necessarily relies on re-observing the same player in later months, so longitudinal analyses operate on a smaller and more selective subset than the full sampled panel. 

```{r Panel Depth Plot}
#| label: fig-panel-depth
#| fig-cap: "The panel is unbalanced: Many players appear briefly; fewer are observed consistently. Lag-based outcomes are only defined for a subset of observations."
#| fig-align: center

panel_len <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, COUNT(DISTINCT month) AS n_months
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    GROUP BY player
  )
  SELECT n_months, COUNT(*) AS n_players
  FROM x
  GROUP BY n_months
  ORDER BY n_months
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(panel_len, aes(x = n_months, y = n_players)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  labs(x = "Months Observed per Player", y = "Players",
       title = "Panel Depth: How Long Players Remain Observable") +
  theme_few()
```

Overall, the data are informative but unevenly supported. Some parts of the sample are much better represented than others, so short-horizon player outcomes should be interpreted with appropriate caution. @sec-methodology and @sec-modeling address these issues more directly.

<!--
Pictured in @fig-delta-rating is without contest the single most perfect Gaussian distribution I have ever seen in a real-world dataset. This is not a parsing mistake, nor the result of some sort of transformation, but a natural consequence of the Glicko-2 rating system employed by Lichess. Both Glicko-2 and its predecessor Glicko assume that player skill – both for individuals *and* for a given population – follows a normal distribution. Because of that, implementations of Glicko systems almost always result in normally-distributed skill ratings, provided the player count is high enough.^[It's important to note that Glicko-based systems don't 'force' ratings to conform to a normal distribution; it's possible for them to fall into any form, but the way the system is designed tends to converge towards normality in most cases.] Practically, this means that $\Delta$ rating should be treated as a noisy outcome requiring careful aggregation, preferring binned summaries over unconstrained smoothing. It also encourages caution when interpreting statistically-significant-yet-tiny effects, as small, downright impractical or meaningless outcomes can still read as significant when dealing with a distribution like this.

Unsurprisingly, @fig-volatility shows that the variance in players' month-to-moth ratings decreases with the number of games played in a given month. Importantly, the figure is log-transformed; though the plot visualizes a linear relationship, the first hundred games or so are comparatively more impactful than the next thousand. This is a relationship that I would expect to see with any rating system – law of large numbers and all – but was something I was expecting from Glicko-2 in particular. On top of rating, Glicko systems also measure uncertainty, which is a Bayesian-style measure of how confident it is in a player's rating. Because uncertainty always reduces as more games are played, it makes sense that this relationship is so clearly present in the data. This figure helps reinforce the need for minimum-games filters (which will reduce heteroskedastic noise) and shows that weighting by games is defensible as precision weighting. It also supports longer-horizon $\Delta$ (over multiple months instead of just one) as a way to increase robustness because it averages noise.



@fig-low-time shows that low-time rate is massively zero-inflated, to the degree that it's difficult to identify a meaningful relationship when modeled continuously; binning is practically a necessity. Not shown directly in the figure is the fact that rapid and classical time controls don't have enough data to be meaningfully modeled on their own; due to how low-time rate is defined in the parser, a much smaller proportion of moves classify as being performed under time pressure.^[Low-time definition: A move is flagged as 'low time' if the remaining clock time after the move satisfies $\text{clock\_after} \le \max\!\left(10,\; 2 \times \text{increment}\right)$ seconds, where $\text{increment}$ is the per-move increment of the game's time control.] This justifies collapsing across time controls via move-weighted aggregations, near-exclusive use of binned metrics (including a 0% bin) instead of smoothers, and a combination of minimum move-row thresholds and n-per-bin reports for defensibility.



Collectively, these diagnostics show that the dataset is (1) imbalanced across time controls (and ratings, though not visualized), (2) highly variable in within-unit support, and (3) noisy in short-horizon outcomes. Therefore, methods should adopt minimum-support thresholds, use precision weights, and rely on binned or aggregated summaries for stable inference.
-->
### Opening Behavior {#sec-eda-opening}

The opening plots suggest considerably more temporal stability than rapid metagame turnover. At the level of the most common named openings, there isn't much evidence of dramatic month-to-month turnover across the two-year sample window; the basic impression is one of gradual change as opposed to rapid metagame cycling. Although the degree of stability differs by time control, the same broad pattern appears across all three formats. Additional time-control-specific plots are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b].

@fig-opening-rating is more informative for interpretation. Although broad temporal drift appears fairly modest, opening share changes more clearly across rating levels. Some openings gain relative share as player rating increases, while others lose it, and those gradients are easier to see than the changes over calendar time. The Pirc and Philidor are especially good examples. Even where the shifts aren't large in absolute terms, the rating structure is clearer than anything suggested by the over-time plots alone.

In summary, the exploratory evidence suggests that opening behavior is better framed as structured choice by rating and format than as rapid metagame turnover over time.

```{r Opening by Rating}
#| label: fig-opening-rating
#| fig-cap: "Opening trends by rating are more interesting. The Pirc and Philidor defenses show particularly interesting movement as player rating increases."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-height: 4

# settings
tc_use <- "blitz"
bin_width <- 200
top_k <- 8             # number of openings to plot
min_bin_total <- 2000  # min player-games in a rating bin

# pick top openings within tc_bucket (weighted by games)
top_openings <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT opening, SUM(games) AS total_games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE tc_bucket = '%s'
      AND opening IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY opening
  )
  SELECT opening
  FROM x
  ORDER BY total_games DESC
  LIMIT %d
", qpath(paths$pom_tc), tc_use, top_k))

open_list <- paste0(
  "('", paste(gsub("'", "''", top_openings$opening), collapse="','"), "')"
)

# compute opening share within rating bins
trend_rating <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH base AS (
    SELECT
      tc_bucket,
      opening,
      avg_rating,
      games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE tc_bucket = '%s'
      AND opening IN %s
      AND opening IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
  ),
  binned AS (
    SELECT
      opening,
      CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating / %d) * %d AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin_lo,
      SUM(games) AS player_games
    FROM base
    GROUP BY opening, rating_bin_lo
  ),
  totals AS (
    SELECT
      rating_bin_lo,
      SUM(player_games) AS bin_total
    FROM binned
    GROUP BY rating_bin_lo
  )
  SELECT
    b.rating_bin_lo,
    (b.rating_bin_lo + %d - 1) AS rating_bin_hi,
    b.opening,
    b.player_games,
    t.bin_total,
    CAST(b.player_games AS DOUBLE) / t.bin_total AS share
  FROM binned b
  JOIN totals t USING (rating_bin_lo)
  WHERE t.bin_total >= %d
  ORDER BY b.rating_bin_lo, b.opening
", qpath(paths$pom_tc), tc_use, open_list,
   bin_width, bin_width, bin_width, min_bin_total))


trend_rating <- trend_rating |>
  mutate(
    rating_bin = paste0(rating_bin_lo, "\u2013", rating_bin_hi),
    rating_bin = factor(rating_bin, levels = unique(rating_bin))
  )

ggplot(trend_rating, aes(x = rating_bin, y = share, color = opening, group = opening)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Rating",
    y = "Share of Player-Games",
    title = paste0("Opening Share by Rating (Blitz)"),
    color = ""
  ) +
  scale_color_few() +
  theme_few() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust=1)
  ) + 
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE))
```

### Time Usage {#sec-eda-time}

The time-usage plots show clearer structure. @fig-time shows a clear difference in thinking time across both time controls and skill levels. Blitz and classical are foils: Stronger players spend less time per move in blitz, but more time per move in classical. Rapid lies somewhere in between. Even without formal modeling, this shows that time control isn't just a background element; it fundamentally changes the relationship between rating and pace.

#| label: fig-time
#| fig-cap: "All three time controls have distinct time-usage patterns as player rating increases."
#| fig-align: center

time_bin <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    floor(avg_rating/100)*100 AS rating_bin,
    AVG(avg_time_spent) AS mean_time_spent,
    SUM(move_rows) AS total_moves
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  HAVING total_moves >= 20000
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc)))

ggplot(time_bin, aes(x=rating_bin, y=mean_time_spent)) +
  geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")), scales="free_y", labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))) +
  labs(x="Player Rating", y="Average Time per Move (Seconds)", title="Thinking Time Varies by Skill and Time Control") +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

@fig-time-allocation is in my opinion one of the most interesting. It breaks down the time-per-move from @fig-time into the amount of time allocated in opening, middlegame, and endgame phases.^[Game phases are defined by the Stockfish chess engine rather than a consistent standard.] Regardless of skill or time control, the consistent throughline is that players spend the most time thinking in the middlegame and the least in the opening, with the endgame in the middle. This is about what I'd expect. The opening has the fewest possible permutations, and is often studied and memorized, and while the end- and middlegames are similar, the former tends to be defined when fewer pieces remain on the board, which reduces complexity and thus thinking time. It sugggests factoring by gamestate may also be helpful when modeling move time as an outcome.

A useful supporting pattern is that the same broad structure remains visible when time use is broken down by game phase, suggesting that the broad time-use gradients in @fig-time are not just artifacts of averaging everything together. For more information, refer to Appendix [-@sec-appendix-b]. All in all, time management does not look one-dimensional. Average pace changes across formats, and the meaning of 'using more time' depends heavily on the time control in question, which makes time usage look like a genuine behavioral outcome rather than a mechanical byproduct of format alone.

## Methodology {#sec-methodology}

This section describes the analytic preparation, feature construction, and modeling framework used in the study. The analysis is observational and non-causal throughout; models are used for description, association, prediction, and exploratory summarization, *not* causal identification.

Because the project combines several research questions across multiple linked datasets, the methodology proceeds in two stages. First, variables are transformed and aligned so that quantities are comparable across players, months, and time controls. Second, we define a set of modeling tasks aligned with the project goals: metagame dynamics, opening popularity, time use, player progression, and player categorization.

All predictive modeling uses forward-in-time data splits. Training data are drawn from earlier months in the sample window, while validation and test data are drawn from later contiguous months. Splitting is performed at the month level so that observations from a given month are never used to predict themselves or earlier periods. This design reduces temporal leakage and makes held-out evaluation more realistic, especially for progression targets defined for future rating change. Where relevant, models are also checked across time-control and rating strata to ensure that conclusions aren't driven by a single format or skill band.

<!--
At the core of this project are three themes, as listed in the @sec-background: (1) descriptive metagame dynamics, (2) how time constraints relate to behavior and performance, and (3) characterization of player types or styles. The analysis is strictly non-causal; models are used for description, association, and prediction under out-of-sample evaluation.

When splitting the data into train and test sets, all predictive modeling uses forward-in-time splits to avoid data leakage. This means that the training set contains earlier months in the sample window, while the validation/test set are a contiguous block of later months that were held out from the training data. This split is applied at the month level so that predictors from any given month are never trained using information from future months. For player progression tasks, where the target is a future rating change, using time-forward splits is essential for keeping evaluation realistic.

When appropriate, models are additionally checked for robustness under time-control and rating-bin stratification, to ensure performance isn't driven by a single skill or time-control band.
-->
### Data Transformations {#sec-methodology-transformations}

The linked analytic tables described in @sec-data operate at different observational units and therefore require additional alignment before modeling. Transformations were implemented to improve comparability across contexts, reduce instability in sparse cells, and construct interpretable predictors for the later analyses.

#### Analytic Alignment and Scaling {#sec-methodology-transformations-alignment}

The project does not rely on a single modeling table. Instead, different tasks use different analytic units, including player-month summaries, player-month-by-time-control summaries, opening-level repertoire tables, metagame month summaries, and move-time summaries. These tables were retained at their native units whenever possible so that each model could be fit on the level most appropriate to its target. As a result, some models operate on aggregate month-level data, while others operate on player-period or opening-period observations.

Rating was sometimes converted from a continuous quantity into bins for descriptive summaries, nonparametric plots, and models that benefited from coarse stratification. This was done primarily to stabilize estimates and improve interpretability in settings where fine-grained rating variation was not necessary. For clustering and other multivariate feature-based analyses, retained numeric inputs were standardized as z-scores so that variables measured on different scales – e.g., seconds, proportions, counts, rating points – would contribute on a comparable basis.

#### Weighting, Thresholds, and Support {#sec-methodology-transformations-weighting}

Many outcomes are rates or shares estimated from cells with unequal support. Some observations are based on large numbers of games or move rows, whereas others are based on very small samples and are correspondingly volatile. For this reason, weighting and support restrictions were used where appropriate.

When player-level quantities needed to be collapsed across time controls, overall summaries were constructed using exposure-based weighting. For example, overall player-month rating was computed as a games-weighted average of time-control-specific average ratings, and overall time-pressure quantities were computed using move-based weighting when derived from move-level summaries. This approach prevents low-volume cells from exerting the same influence as high-volume cells when constructing cross-format summaries.

Minimum-support thresholds were also applied in settings where extremely sparse observations would otherwise dominate. Depending on the task, these thresholds were defined in terms of games per player-month, games per opening cell, or move rows per time-use summary. These filters were not intended to alter the substantive population under study, but rather to limit the influence of cells whose estimates were too unstable to reliably interpret.

#### Derived Features and Missingness {#sec-methodology-transformations-derived}

Several interpretable features were constructed from the player-opening and time-use tables for use in the progression and categorization analyses. These features were intended to summarize broad aspects of player behavior.

Repertoire breadth was measured using opening diversity, defined as the number of distinct openings used within the relevant period. Repertoire concentration was summarized using the share of games allocated to the player’s most-used opening. Repertoire adjustment was captured in two related ways—  an indicator for whether the most-played opening changed from the previous month, and measures of month-to-month repertoire churn based on changes in opening-share vectors and the appearance of newly used openings. Time-use behavior was summarized using variables such as average time spent per move, upper-tail move-time summaries, opening-phase time allocation, and low-time frequency.^[Low-time definition: A move is flagged as 'low time' if the remaining clock time after the move satisfies $\text{clock\_after} \le \max\!\left(10,\; 2 \times \text{increment}\right)$ seconds, where $\text{increment}$ is the per-move increment of the game's time control.]

Some time-use variables were structurally missing rather than randomly absent. In particular, endgame time measures are often unavailable because many games do not reach a computer-defined endgame phase.^[<Placeholder: Potential note here elaborating on the reason why?>] These missing values therefore reflect game structure rather than arbitrary loss of data. Models using phase-specific variables either handled these cases explicitly or restricted analysis to observations for which the relevant phase was meaningfully defined.


<!--

Transformations serve to stabilize noisy estimates, make quantities comparable across players and contexts, and construct interpretable features aligned with all three research topics. Different transformations are applied for different purposes.

#### Aggregation-Level Alignment {#sec-aggregation}

Rather than a single, monolithic dataset, this project handles several datasets aligned to differing observational units. Strictly speaking, this alignment occurs during the data pipeline itself rather than a formal, pre-modeling cleaning step but it's important to note nonetheless. Broadly, the observational units for each table can be separated into four categories: metagame (population-level games), player outcomes (player-level games), time usage, and opening repertoire. This, however, is an oversimplification; please refer to @sec-data for more detail.

#### Binning and Standardization

To support nonparametric EDA and stable estimation, rating is often binned for plots and stratified summaries— several of which have already been featured in @sec-eda. For clustering (player type/style discovery), features are standardized using z-scores so that variables measured on different scales (e.g., seconds, proportions, counts) contribute in a comparable manner.

#### Exposure Weighting and Time-Control-Collapsed Quantities

As displayed by @fig-coverage in @sec-eda, in some contexts it's justifiable to collapse observations across time controls, particularly where classical is concerned. When a model needs 'overall' player-month measures rather than those specific to a given time control, overall rating is constructed as a games-weighted average of `avg_rating` across time controls. Similarly, overall time-trouble rate becomes an average of `low_time_rate` across time controls, weighted by move rows. This prevents the volume disparity between time controls from disproportionately influencing aggregated quantities.

#### Reliability Thresholds

Many variables are rates estimated from finite samples. Often, these sample sizes are extremely small, increasing volatility. In order to reduce such noise, minimum thresholds for observation count may be applied; player-month observations may require a minimum number of games per player, time-use observations a number of move-rows, and opening-level estimates a number of games per group. This filtering may still be applied even if the model or models being fit don't explicitly require it to function (or as part of a fundamental model assumption) to ensure that modeled signals are not dominated by small-sample volatility.

#### Derived Features

A set of interpetable style features is constructed from player-opening and time-use tables for use in type discovery and player-progression models. Similarly to @sec-aggregation, some of these features were created during the data pipeline itself, while others are derived directly from them. These include:

- Repertoire breath, measured by `opening_diversity`.
- Repertoire concentration, computed as a share of games in the most-played opening from `player_opening_month`.
- Opening switching, indicated by whether `top_opening` differs from the previous month.
- Repertoire churn, measured jointly as:
  - The distance between consecutive-month opening-share vectors.
  - The share of games in brand new openings relative to the month prior.
- Time-pressure behavior, based on a combination of `low_time_rate` plus summaries like `avg_time_spent`, `p90_time_spent`, and `avg_time_opening`.

For more information on pre-existing features, see @sec-data.

#### Missingness

Finally, phase-specific time metrics are often missing for structural reasons. Almost always, the phase missing is endgame, as many games never reach a computer-defined endgame due to resignation or blundered, early losses. Models that use phase variables either include explicit missingness handling or analyze phases separately with appropriate inclusion rules.

### Modeling Tasks and Candidate Specifications {#sec-methodology-models}

Because this paper addresses several distinct questions, candidate models are organized by modeling task rather than abstract model family. Each task corresponds to a substantive question, a natural observational unit, and a set of candidate specifications suited to that problem. Formal model comparison and retention are deferred to @sec-modeling. The present section instead defines the role of each modeling task and the types of specifications considered.

<!--
Because this project aims to explore a variety of questions by modeling on multiple datasets, strictly categorizing models by family makes little sense.^[Here, I define "model family" as sets of  models operating under similar principles and fundamental assumptions (e.g., general linear models, tree-based models, etc.), whereas "model category" refers to the five groupings of models I specifically define for this paper.] Were there a single theme and associated dataset, doing so would make it easy to illustrate exactly how each type of model contributes to the project's singular goal. In this case, however, I think it more appropriate to categorize models by their goal; to define them by the questions they intend to answer and the methods they'll use in seeking them.^[It should be noted that this form of model categorization allows for slight overlap between model families; some families may be used by multiple categories of model.] 
-->


#### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics}

Metagame-dynamics models were used to describe how aggregate ecosystem measures changed across month and time control. These models focus on population-level structure rather than individual players. Depending on the outcome, the primary observational units were either month-by-time-control summaries or opening-by-month-by-time-control summaries.

The main outcomes in this task include concentration and diversity measures, draw rate, upset rate, average game length, and opening share. Predictors primarily include month, time control, and their interactions. Candidate specifications included weighted linear models for macro outcomes and multinomial models for opening composition, with simpler opening-by-opening share models considered as descriptive comparisons.

The motivation for using more than one specification in this task is straightforward. Some metagame quantities, such as concentration or average moves, are scalar month-level summaries and are naturally modeled with weighted regressions. Opening composition, by contrast, is inherently compositional— increases in one opening’s share imply decreases elsewhere. Models that account for this compositional structure were therefore considered when the goal was to describe substitution within the opening ecosystem.


<!--
Temporal dynamics and environment (time is the key axis)


The goal of metagame models are to quantify how aggregate metagame metrics vary across factors such as time and format. The primary observational unit is `meta_opening_month_tc`, while response variables include `share` and outcome rates (e.g., `white_win_rate`). The model families which fall under this category include generalized additive models (GAM) and weighted linear models (WLM), as well as multinomial models. 

GAM and WLM models are useful because they produce simple, easy-to-read trend estimates. The incorporation of weights let high-support opening-month cells impact the fit more than small, noisy cells, and GAM-style smoothing allows for nonlinear time trends without forcing a specific form. Both are strong at tracking a small set of common openings over time (which, given the EDA, is very relevant #ref) while remaining easy to justify and visualize. Importantly, because opening shares are bounded and compositional, these models can only ever approximate the true structure of opening share, meaning that results will necessarily be biased or even potentially spurious.

Multinomial models exist to solve the problem of compositional variables. By modeling on log-odds and log-ratios, they avoid predicting impossible shares ($\notin 0 < x < 1$); in essence, they're capable of implicitly understanding that if one opening goes up, others must go down. This provides interpretable effects for opening adoption relative to a specific baseline, meaning they're best when relative substitution between openings is of import. Multinomial models tend to work better when modeling a large portion of a distribution (rather than just the top k), but as a consequence are more complicated to both implement and interpret.

Combined, these models attempt to ask questions about the state of the metagame – the Lichess 'ecosystem' –  and its evolution rather than just fitting adoption curves. 
-->

#### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity}

Opening-popularity models were used to describe how opening choice varied with player strength and time control. This task overlaps with metagame analysis but is narrower in scope; rather than modeling the ecosystem as a whole, it focuses specifically on opening-adoption patterns.

The primary observational unit for this task is the month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin opening summary. Outcomes are opening shares or opening-use counts, and the key predictors are rating level, time control, month, and rating-by-format interactions. Candidate specifications included pooled multinomial models as the main compositional approach, along with count-based and weighted share models as lower-complexity alternatives.

This task treats opening popularity as a structured choice problem. The multinomial framework is useful because it represents the full set of retained openings jointly, allowing probabilities to coherently shift across categories. Simpler single-opening models remain useful as descriptive checks, but fail to fully represent substitution across openings and as such play a secondary role in this modeling category.

<!--
Skill-conditioned preferences (rating is the key axis). Update first paragraph now that we're using `pom_tc` instead.


The goal of opening-popularity models is to describe how opening preferences differ by player skill and time control. You'll notice that this goal shares substantial overlap with that of metagame models, and indeed, opening popularity is a subset of metagame dynamics. The core difference between the two is that opening-popularity models exclusively target the adoption rate of openings at the expense of all other metagame descriptors; they care not for the diversity of the opening pool, or how outcome rates, game length, and rating gaps shift, for instance. While both use `meta_opening_month_tc` as an observational unit, popularity models prefer to treat each opening separately (top-k) or as a compositional set focused on `share`. Models in this category include multinomial models, count models, and weighted regression.

Contrary to the metagame category, multinomial models are front and center for opening popularity because the target is explicitly compositional. Metagame models seek to observe large-scale patterns more than anything, so in their case it's possible to get away with using multinomials as a backup for increased accuracy, but when it comes to opening popularity there's no real excuse. Multinomial choice models build player-game as a categorical choice, producing probabilities of choosing each opening as a function of things like rating and time control. They're computationally heavy, but are worth the price if they have access to enough data.

Count models such as poisson and negative binomial are a simpler answer to the same problem, treating observed opening use as counts out of a total number of games. By applying an offset (e.g., taking the log of total games), they can effectively model rates while remaining in count space. Negative binomial can handle overdispersion, which is common in count data. Their main advantage over multinomial models is their ability to produce interpretable, multiplicative effects, or rate ratios, which allows for another angle of analysis.

Finally, weighted regression on `share` takes the 'simple is best' philosophy to an extreme. Just as in the prior section, they don't enforce composition, meaning they're liable to misbehave at the boundaries if used for extrapolation; they can't replace multinomial or count models and only serve as an approximation. They remain for much the same reasons as before: they're easy to implement, easy to explain, and good when the only goal is a half-decent descriptive model focused on top openings. Weighted regression certainly won't be the star of the show, but it's such a simple addition that it costs nothing to include.

Together, these models seek to hone in on opening popularity with a higher degree of specificity than the metagame models, each through varying levels of complexity.

-->

#### Time Use {#sec-time-use}

Time-use models were used to characterize how time allocation varied across skill and time control. These models treat time management as a behavioral outcome rather than as a byproduct of format alone. Two related targets were emphasized— average time use and low-time frequency.

Depending on the target, the primary observational units were either player-month-by-time-control summaries or month-level time-use summaries. Outcomes include average time spent per move, upper-tail move-time summaries, phase-specific averages, and the proportion of moves taken in low-time states. The central predictors are player rating, time control, and in some cases their interaction, with month included where temporal adjustment is needed.

Candidate specifications included additive and interaction regressions for mean time-use outcomes, robust or quantile-based alternatives for heavy-tailed variables, and bounded-outcome models for low-time frequency. The reason for considering multiple mean-modeling strategies is that time-use data can be skewed and sensitive to outliers, while low-time frequency is both bounded and concentrated near zero. Different specifications were considered depending on whether the main challenge was nonlinearity, heavy tails, or bounded proportion structure.

<!--
Time use models attempt to characterize the way time allocation varies across skill and time control. Observational units are `player_time_month_tc` for player-level behavior and `moves_month_tc` for macro behavior. Response variables include time spent, time management, pressure, and phase allocation, while predictors primarily consist of `avg_rating` and `tc_bucket`. Three related pairs of models populate this category: additive- and interaction regression, robust- and quantile regression, and beta- and logistic-style modeling.

Additive regression and interaction regression provide a clean separation between skill effects and constraint effects. Additive regression assumes each predictor contributes its own effect, and that those effects simply add up, best for when predictors are believed to act independently of one another. They also tend to be a substitute for interaction regression when there's not enough data. Interaction regression, as the name implies, allows the effect of one predictor to depend on the level of another predictor. Both are relatively easy to interpret.

Robust regression and quantile regression are useful in situations when ordinary least squares (OLS) is a poor fit. Notably, both solve different problems. Robust regression still estimates the conditional mean like OLS, but makes it less sensitive to outliers, whereas quantile regression breaks the mold by estimating a conditional quantile (e.g., median, 90th percentile, etc.) rather than the mean. As a consequence, they must also be interpreted slightly differently, as they ask how predictors shift a percentile rather than the mean. They're valuable for modeling time use because time-related variables often present heavy tails, which these models are better equipped to handle.

Beta and logistic modeling are along for the ride because of a specific problem. Namely, `low_time_rate` is bounded and almost always piles up at 0. Both beta and logit-style approaches keep predictions bounded in [0, 1], handling proportion structure better than OLS, the core difference between the two being that logistic modeling uses a binary response (or a count of successes out of a total number of trials), while beta modeling uses a continuous proportion between 0 and 1. By binning low-time rate, it's possible to produce stable summaries that avoid smoothing failures, making for a more-easily-defensible model

Together, these models thoroughly explore several different methods of time-use analysis. The reason this section contains three pairs of complimentary models rather than just the 'better' of each pair is that the EDA did not produce conclusive enough evidence to justify jumping straight to a smaller subset of model options; the data is complex enough that a simple visual inspection was insufficient for ruling out one choice or the other, and so the most reliable solution is to test them all.
-->

#### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression}

Player-progression models were used to relate current-month behavior to later rating movement. These models ask whether within-player changes in activity, game structure, repertoire behavior, and related features are associated with subsequent changes in rating over short horizons.

The baseline observational unit is the player-month table, optionally joined to time-control or repertoire summaries when the required predictors are available. Outcomes are defined as future rating change over one- and three-month horizons, along with an absolute-change outcome used to summarize movement magnitude without direction. Predictors include current rating, game volume, average game length, repertoire breadth, repertoire concentration, repertoire adjustment, and selected time-use features where support permits.

Candidate specifications included regularized linear models, panel-data models, and tree-based regressions. Regularized models were considered because many player-level predictors are correlated. Panel models were considered because the data are longitudinal and repeated within players. Tree-based models were considered as flexible predictive benchmarks capable of capturing nonlinearities and interactions without extensive manual specification. Because this task is explicitly forward-looking, realistic temporal splitting is especially important; the model must predict later rating movement using only information available at the current month.

<!--
Player-progression models are straightforward: They wish to relate a player's current-month behavior to future rating change. The purpose of this category is simple, asking if it's possible to isolate certain factors that prove to have a marked effect on a player's growth— positive *or* negative. The baseline observational unit for these models is `player_month`, which can be stratified by time control (`player_month_tc`) or joined to other tables for additional information (e.g., `player_time_month_tc` or `player_opening_month_tc`). The response variables are derived from `avg_rating` and all represent $\Delta rating$ in some form. Horizon spans may differ (i.e., rating change over spans greater than a single month), and constructing a stability model using $|\Delta|$ is also possible. Predictors include the number of games and moves played during a given timespan, style proxies, and time-use features, controlled by baseline rating and other fixed effects. Comprising this category are model families such as regularized linear models, mixed-/fixed effects models, and tree-based regression.

Regularized linear models (ridge, lasso, elastic net) help account for the fact that this category's predictors are correlated. Regularization stabilizes these estimates. Ridge regression is good for prediction under multicollinearity, and lasso, though perhaps less relevant here is good for feature selection. Elastic net is a hybrid of the two. As a whole, they should provide a strong baseline predictive model without sacrificing interpretability.

Fixed effects models and mixed (random) effects models are good at handling longitudinal data, though they differ in how they handle time-invariant predictors. The former controls for time-invariant differences without attempting to predict their effects, while the latter tries to estimate said effects. Fixed effects push towards within-player identification, while mixed effects will pool players to improve stability. Crucially, mixed effects models assume that unit intercepts are uncorrelated to the regressors, which can't be reasonably assumed with this data. Fixed effects models are likely to be the better performing of the two (if non-fixed models even pass muster at all), though the implementation of something like a correlated random effects (Mundlak) model might help bridge the gap.

Tree-based regression both naturally captures nonlinearities and thresholds in the data and automatically handles interactions without explicit specification. They're best for exploratory prediction and detecting complex feature relationships. As with all tree-based models, this comes at the cost of interpretability; they require interpretation tools such as feature importance, partial dependence plots, individual conditional expectation plots, et cetera, and even then struggle to match the interpretability of more-straightforward models.

Together, these models account for the varying facets of longitudinal player-level modeling in order to identify the best angle to attack the problem from.
-->
#### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization}

Player-categorization models were used to summarize recurring behavioral profiles in player-month observations. This task is exploratory rather than inferential. The goal is not to estimate latent causal types, but to determine whether broad behavioral configurations can be recovered from performance, repertoire, and activity features.

The natural observational unit is a joined player-month-by-time-control table containing performance measures, repertoire summaries, and other standardized features. Inputs include rating, rating differential, game length, outcome rates, repertoire breadth, repertoire concentration, repertoire adjustment, and selected activity measures. Time-use variables were considered where coverage allowed, but their inclusion depended on support in the merged sample.

Candidate specifications included dimensionality-reduction methods and clustering algorithms. Dimensionality reduction was used to summarize major axes of behavioral variation and to inspect whether lower-dimensional structure was visible in the data. Clustering methods were used to partition the feature space into interpretable behavioral groupings. Because the goal of this task is descriptive summarization, later evaluation emphasizes balance, stability, and interpretability rather than formal inference.

<!--
As the name implies, player-categorization models want to categorize players. More specifically, they seek to identify clusters using behavioral features, stratifying by rating and format, and observing for stability. This is by far the most nebulous of the model categories because they're primarily exploratory in nature; rather than beginning with pre-defined player archetypes and asking how their performance differs, these models ask which style clusters (if any) can be identified in the first place. The most straightforward observational unit is a join between `player_month_tc`, `player_time_month_tc`, and repertoire-derived features, and inputs include performance, outcomes, repertoire breadth, time use, and general context. The core model families in this category are dimensionality reduction and clustering, though additional modeling becomes possible after playstyle has been categorized.

Dimensionality reduction methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) provide low-dimensional representation. PCA yields interpretable axes and helps with noise reduction, whereas UMAP is useful for visual separations and nonlinear manifolds. PCA is a linear method which tries to preserve large-scale structure, while UMAP is a nonlinear method prefers preserving cluster separation. Dimensionality reduction is good at for summarizing multi-feature space *before* clustering or visualization, which should prove helpful in the case of a very broad 'style space'.

Clustering methods (e.g., k-means, hierarchical, GMM) are potentially capable of turning continuous player-behavior into discrete, describable archetypes. K-means clustering is fast, but requires tuning towards an unknown k. Hierarchical clustering is tree-based and doesn't require a known k, but requires a dendrogram for interpretation, and Gaussian mixture models (GMM) creates clusters of varying sizes with associated membership probabilities, which is useful if player archetypes overlap. 

Though perhaps not within the scope of this project, dimensionality reduction and clustering are notable as a potential method of creating discrete types for downstream modeling. Once each player-month has a type, it becomes possible to study stability and movement between types or perform supervised follow-up using type labels (e.g., as predictors of progression).
  
Together, these models explore the bounds of player-archetype/playstyle categorization.
-->

### Summary {#sec-methodology-summary}

Taken together, these transformations and modeling tasks define the analytic structure of the paper. The transformations align linked datasets, stabilize sparse quantities, and produce interpretable features for later use. The modeling tasks then organize the empirical questions into five domains: ecosystem-level metagame change, opening choice, time management, longitudinal progression, and exploratory behavioral profiling.

## Modeling {#sec-modeling}

This section compares the candidate models introduced in @sec-methodology-models and identifies the specifications retained for the remainder of the analysis. The purpose here is not to present substantive findings, but to narrow a broader set of candidate models to a smaller set of primary specifications for each modeling task. Substantive interpretation is deferred to @sec-results.

Model retention is based on four considerations: inferential suitability, held-out predictive adequacy, robustness to reasonable specification changes, and interpretability. These criteria do not apply identically to every modeling problem. In some cases, the retained model is primarily inferential; in others, it is better understood as descriptive or predictive. This distinction is especially important for exploratory methods such as clustering, which are useful for summarizing structure in the data but are not treated as a basis for inferential claims.

Because a large number of models were fit during development, the body of this section focuses on retention decisions and the reasons for them. Detailed predictive comparisons, robustness checks, and supplemental diagnostics are reported in Appendices [-@sec-appendix-c], [-@sec-appendix-d], [-@sec-appendix-e], and [-@sec-appendix-f].

### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics-2}

Metagame dynamics were modeled at two related levels. First, aggregate ecosystem and game-environment outcomes were modeled at the month-by-time-control level. These macro outcomes included opening concentration and diversity, along with draw rate, upset rate, and average moves. Second, opening composition itself was modeled separately by time control using specifications designed for compositional outcomes.

For the macro outcomes, weighted linear models were retained as the primary inferential framework. These specifications provided a direct and interpretable way to estimate time trends and time-control differences while accommodating unequal support across month-by-format cells. Because the macro series are observed over time, inference relied on heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors.

<!-- consider using times symbol instead of cdot for equations to avoid confusing cdots with periods. -->

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{tc,t}
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1 t
+
\beta_2 \,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3 \,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4 \, t \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5 \, t \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}=\mathrm{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_{tc,t}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained macro metagame model. Here, $Y_{tc,t}$ denotes a month-by-time-control metagame outcome, such as HHI concentration, effective number of openings, draw rate, upset rate, or average moves. Inference used Newey--West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-macro}
\end{figure}
```

Opening composition required a different retained model because opening shares are inherently compositional. Candidate models included weighted fixed-effects share regressions, GAM-based share regressions, and multinomial specifications fit separately by time control. The multinomial models were retained as the primary inferential basis for compositional change because they represent the full opening set jointly and therefore respect the substitution structure of opening shares. By contrast, the share-based alternatives model openings one at a time and are better treated as descriptive comparisons than as primary inferential models.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_t = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{k,t})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{j,t})}, \\
\eta_{k,t}
&=
\alpha_k + \beta_k t,
\qquad k=1,\dots,K.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained multinomial metagame-composition model, fit separately by time control. Here, $Y_t$ denotes the opening category at month $t$, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories.}
\label{fig:eq-metagame-multinomial}
\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks further supported this division of labor. Changes to the retained opening set altered predictive difficulty in the expected way, but did not overturn the main directional patterns of the multinomial results. Detailed comparisons and robustness checks for both the macro and compositional models are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].

### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity-2}

Opening popularity was modeled primarily as a compositional problem. The main inferential candidate was a pooled multinomial model fit to month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin cells, with openings aggregated into a retained top-$k$ set plus an “Other” category after sparse cells were excluded. This specification used rating bin, time control, month index, and rating-by-time-control interactions to model opening composition across player-strength strata and formats.

Per-opening negative binomial and weighted least squares models were also fit as lower-complexity alternatives. These models were useful as sensitivity checks because they allowed individual openings to be examined one at a time, but that same feature limited their suitability as the primary model for opening choice. Since they do not model the opening set jointly, they cannot represent substitution across openings in a fully coherent way.

The pooled multinomial model was retained as the primary specification for this subsection. The main reasons were structural appropriateness and competitive held-out performance. It aligned most directly with the compositional form of the outcome while remaining interpretable enough for downstream use in @sec-results. The simpler one-opening alternatives remained useful as supporting checks, but not as the main retained specification.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(Y_i = k)
&=
\frac{\exp(\eta_{ik})}
{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\eta_{ij})}, \\
\eta_{ik}
&=
\alpha_k
+
\beta_{1k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i
+
\beta_{2k}\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_{3k}\,t_i
+
\beta_{4k}\,\mathrm{RatingBin}_i
\cdot
\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained pooled multinomial opening-popularity model. Here, $Y_i$ denotes the opening category for month-by-time-control-by-rating-bin cell $i$, $t_i$ is the month index, and $k$ indexes the retained opening categories, including "Other".}
\label{fig:eq-opening-popularity}
\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks did not materially alter that decision. Allowing modest nonlinear flexibility in rating changed held-out fit only slightly, while greater flexibility in time did not improve performance enough to justify additional complexity. Varying the number of explicitly modeled openings produced the expected tradeoff between simpler and harder prediction problems, but did not change the broader retention logic. Full model comparisons and supporting diagnostics for this subsection are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].

### Time Use {#sec-time-use-2}

Time-use modeling was organized around two related targets— average time use and low-time frequency. Because these outcomes differ in scale and distribution, they were evaluated separately rather than forced into a single retained model family.

For average time use, candidate specifications were compared at both the macro month level and the player-month level. At each level, additive models were compared against interaction specifications that allowed the relationship between rating and time use to vary by time control. The interaction specifications outperformed the corresponding additive alternatives at both analytic levels, even if the numerical improvement was modest. Those gains were directionally consistent and supported the conclusion that a common rating slope across formats was too restrictive for mean time-use modeling. The interaction forms were therefore retained as the primary models for average time use.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AvgTime}_i
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{Rating}_i \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{Rating}_i \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\}
+
\varepsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained player-level mean time-use model. Here, $\mathrm{AvgTime}_i$ denotes average time spent for observation $i$, and the interaction terms allow the rating slope to vary by time control.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-mean}
\end{figure}
```

For low-time frequency, the main comparison was between a fractional quasibinomial specification and a binomial approximation. Since predictive performance did not clearly distinguish the two, model retention was decided on inferential suitability and outcome structure. The fractional quasibinomial was retained because it is better matched to a bounded proportion outcome observed at the cell level, especially when the outcome is concentrated near zero. The binomial approximation remains a useful sensitivity check, but not the primary retained model.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}\!\left(\mathbb{E}[L_i \mid X_i]\right)
&=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{Rating}_i
+
\beta_2\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Classical}\}
+
\beta_3\,\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{tc}_i=\mathrm{Rapid}\},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained fractional low-time model. Here, $L_i \in [0,1]$ denotes low-time frequency for observation $i$.}
\label{fig:eq-timeuse-lowtime}
\end{figure}
```

Robustness checks supported both retention decisions. Alternative functional forms produced only limited changes in held-out fit, suggesting that the retained models were not being selected solely because of a narrow specification choice. Detailed comparisons and diagnostics for the time-use models are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-d].

### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression-2}

Player-progression models were designed to assess whether month-$t$ player behavior could be used to predict subsequent rating movement under a forward-in-time design. Three targets were retained for evaluation: 1-month rating change, 3-month rating change, and absolute 1-month rating change. The 3-month target is based on a smaller sample because it requires observing the same player several months later, whereas the 1-month targets preserve substantially more observations. This difference in available support is important context for later comparisons across targets.

The main inferential candidate in this subsection was a player fixed-effects model fit to the player-month panel. This choice followed directly from the substantive goal of the task—  isolating within-player associations between current-month behavior and later rating movement. The baseline feature set included current rating, game volume, average moves, opening diversity, top-opening concentration, and an indicator for whether the player switched their most-played opening. Ridge regression and random forest models were also fit as predictive benchmarks.

Across the retained targets, the player fixed-effects specifications provided the strongest overall combination of longitudinal appropriateness, inferential usefulness, and out-of-sample performance. This made the fixed-effects family the clearest retained direction for the progression task. The predictive benchmarks remained useful for comparison, but did not outperform the panel-based specification.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
Y_{it}^{(h)}
&=
\alpha_i
+
\beta_1\,\mathrm{AvgRating}_{it}
+
\beta_2\,\mathrm{Games}_{it}
+
\beta_3\,\mathrm{AvgMoves}_{it} \\
&\quad
+
\beta_4\,\mathrm{OpeningDiversity}_{it}
+
\beta_5\,\mathrm{TopOpeningShare}_{it}
+
\beta_6\,\mathrm{SwitchedOpening}_{it}
+
\varepsilon_{it},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Generic form of the retained player fixed-effects progression model, where $Y_{it}^{(h)} \in \{\Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+1}, \Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+3}, |\Delta \mathrm{Rating}_{i,t+1}|\}$.}
\label{fig:eq-progression-fe-generic}
\end{figure}
```

Sensitivity checks further supported that choice. Adding collapsed time-use features on the common-support sample did not improve performance enough to justify the accompanying loss of coverage, and allowing rating to vary nonlinearly produced only a small change relative to the baseline fit. Additional checks also suggested that absorbing common month shocks through added month fixed effects did not improve fit enough to outweigh the cost in simplicity. Full predictive comparisons and supporting robustness checks for this subsection are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-e].
