### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization-2}

The goal of the player-categorization task was not to identify latent player "types" in a strong inferential sense, but to retain a descriptive specification that could summarize broad behavioral structure in player-month-time-control observations. For that reason, model retention in this subsection emphasized sample coverage, cluster balance, stability, and interpretability rather than formal inferential criteria.

The candidate clustering sample provided complete coverage for repertoire features but only sparse overlap for stable time-use features in the joined design. This made time use unsuitable as a core clustering input in the retained specification. Instead, the retained feature set focused on standardized performance, outcome, repertoire, and activity variables, with time-use measures treated as potential downstream overlays rather than direct inputs to the clustering algorithm.

Candidate descriptive approaches included $k$-means clustering, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixture clustering, and dimensionality-reduction methods used in a supporting role. The retained specification used $k$-means with $k = 6$ on the standardized core-plus-repertoire feature set. This solution was preferred because it provided a reasonably balanced partition, used the best-supported merged sample, and remained straightforward to interpret as a descriptive segmentation.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\small
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\min_{C_1,\dots,C_6}
\sum_{k=1}^{6}
\sum_{i \in C_k}
\left\| x_i - \mu_k \right\|^2,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
\caption{Retained $k$-means clustering objective for player categorization. Here, $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ denotes the standardized feature vector for observation $i$, $C_k$ denotes cluster $k$, and $\mu_k$ denotes the centroid of cluster $k$.}
\label{fig:eq-categorization-kmeans}
\end{figure}
```

The robustness and stability checks supported treating the retained clustering solution as useful, but only in a descriptive sense. Relative to the core-only alternative, the core-plus-repertoire feature set yielded a more balanced solution. Repeated $k$-means fits under the retained specification also converged to the same partition, indicating very strong initialization stability. At the same time, agreement with alternative clustering algorithms was only moderate, silhouette values were modest, and month-to-month agreement for overlapping players was limited. These diagnostics suggest that the retained segmentation captures real structure, but not sharply-separated or highly-persistent latent classes. Detailed specification, comparison, and stability diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-f].

The retained solution captures meaningful differences across both general performance characteristics and opening-related behavior. Table @ref(tab:categorization-performance-profiles) shows that the clusters differ in average rating, rating differential, average moves, and win rate, indicating that the segmentation is not simply reproducing a single skill ordering. Table \ref{tab:categorization-repertoire-profiles} shows additional differences in opening diversity, concentration, and opening-switching behavior, which suggests that repertoire structure is an important part of the retained clustering solution. In particular, some clusters are characterized by broad and diverse opening usage, whereas others are defined more by concentrated repertoires or high switching rates. Log-transformed activity measures were also included in the retained clustering design to reduce the influence of heavy-tailed count variables (see @sec-appendix).



Robustness and stability checks support treating the retained solution as useful, but only in a descriptive sense. As shown in Table \ref{tab:categorization-robustness}, the richer core-plus-repertoire feature set produced a more balanced clustering solution than the core-only alternative. Repeated $k$-means fits under the retained specification converged to the same partition, indicating effectively perfect initialization stability. At the same time, agreement with hierarchical clustering and Gaussian mixture clustering was only moderate, silhouette values were modest, and month-to-month agreement for overlapping players was limited. So, while these diagnostics suggest that the retained segmentation captures real structure in the data, they also suggest that this structure is neither sharply separated nor highly persistent over time.



Dimensionality-reduction methods were used in a supporting role rather than as retained models in their own right. PCA provided a more interpretable low-dimensional summary of the dominant axes of variation in the standardized feature space, while UMAP offered a nonlinear view of local neighborhood structure. Their role here is the same as that of the alternative clustering algorithms—  not to replace the retained clustering specification, but to help assess whether the descriptive segmentation corresponds to visible structure in the player-behavior space.

Ultimately, the retained player-categorization model should be understood as a practical descriptive device. It provides a reproducible way to summarize broad playstyle variation across player-month observations, and the associated diagnostics suggest that the resulting clusters are usable as behavior profiles for downstream description. They are not, however, treated here as definitive latent classes or as a basis for inferential claims about underlying player types.

-->

### Summary {#sec-results-summary}

The retained models define a common analytic strategy across our five empirical domains. Weighted linear and multinomial models were retained for metagame dynamics depending on whether the target was macro or compositional; a pooled multinomial model was retained for opening popularity; interaction-based mean models and a fractional quasibinomial were retained for time use; player fixed-effects models were retained for progression; and a k-means clustering solution based on core-plus-repertoire features was retained for player categorization.

## Results {#sec-results}

This section presents the substantive findings from the retained models described in @sec-modeling. The aim is no longer to compare candidate specifications, but to interpret the model outputs. Accordingly, the section emphasizes interpretable summaries of model output, including estimated effects, representative predicted values, and descriptive profile summaries where appropriate. Additional robustness checks and supplemental diagnostics are reported in Appendices [-@sec-appendix-c], [-@sec-appendix-d], [-@sec-appendix-e], and [-@sec-appendix-f].

### Metagame Dynamics {#sec-metagame-dynamics-3}

The retained metagame models indicate that the opening ecosystem broadened over the study period, although the magnitude of that broadening differed across time controls. The clearest evidence concerns concentration and diversity. Across formats, opening use became less concentrated and the effective number of openings increased, which together indicate gradual metagame diversification rather than convergence onto a narrower set of dominant choices.

Table \ref{tab:metagame-macro-estimates} provides the main inferential summary for the retained macro models. In the baseline format, HHI concentration declined over time while the effective number of openings increased, and both trends were larger in rapid and classical than in blitz. These paired results are substantively aligned—  declining concentration and rising effective diversity describe the same underlying shift toward a broader opening ecosystem. The interaction terms matter here because the rate of diversification was not uniform across formats. Relative to blitz, the broadening was more pronounced in rapid and strongest in classical.

By contrast, the retained macro models provide much weaker evidence for systematic time trends in draw rate and average moves. Those outcomes appear comparatively stable over the sample window. Upset rate shows some evidence of a modest positive baseline trend, but that signal is weaker and less consistent across time controls than the concentration and diversity results. This suggests that metagame structure changed more clearly than the broader game environment did.

Overall, the metagame results point to gradual diversification as opposed to convergence. The strongest findings concern ecosystem structure itself, where openings became less concentrated and more diverse, especially in slower formats. The compositional results suggest that this broadening reflects diffuse redistribution across the opening ecosystem rather than a dramatic surge by any single named opening, with some of the increase appearing to occur in the long tail of less-common choices. Changes in draw rate, upset rate, and average moves were much less pronounced, so the main story here is structural broadening in opening choice. Additional metagame comparisons, compositional checks, and supplemental results are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-c].

All in all, at the ecosystem level, the metagame became less concentrated and more diverse over time, and those structural changes differed in severity across time controls. ### Opening Popularity {#sec-opening-popularity-3}

The retained opening-popularity model shows clear differences in opening choice across rating bins and time controls. The most visible pattern is the increasing share of the residual "Other" category as player strength rises.

@fig-opening-popularity-results provides the clearest visual summary of this pattern. In both blitz and rapid, the predicted share of the “Other” category increases with rating. This implies that stronger players devote a greater proportion of their games to openings outside the explicitly retained top set. That result does not mean the named openings cease to matter; rather, it means the opening ecosystem becomes less concentrated around the same small group of common labeled choices as rating rises.

Temporal changes are present, but modest in magnitude. This again points away from a story of dramatic named-opening turnover and toward one of distributed compositional change.

The substantive takeaway is that opening choice is highly structured, but most of that structure is cross-sectional as opposed to temporal. Rating and time control organize the opening landscape more strongly than month-to-month drift does. Over time, the opening ecosystem shifts, but the magnitude of that shift is much smaller than the difference between lower- and higher-rated opening distributions. ### Time Use {#sec-time-use-3}

The retained time-use models show that average pacing and low-time pressure capture related but distinct aspects of chess behavior. Across the retained specifications, the most consistent result is that the relationship between rating and average time use differs by time control, while low-time frequency rises with rating in every format.

@fig-time-use-results summarizes these two patterns. For average time spent per move, the rating gradient is negative in blitz but positive in rapid and classical. Higher-rated players therefore move faster on average in blitz, but spend more time per move in slower formats. This means that there is no single monotone relationship between skill and pacing. Instead, the behavioral meaning of a player's use of time depends on the format in which it occurs.

<!-- I do not yet have coefficients/model estimates, so currently have some placeholders 

This category of models characterizes how players allocate time and experience time pressure across rating and time control; time use is being treated as a behavioral outcome that may vary by skill and the structure of the format. Two different models were retained for this category: interaction-based mean models for average time use, and a fractional quasibinomial model for low-time frequency. Average time use was modeled separately at the macro and player-month levels, but the results found in this section are taken from the player-level interaction model. Across the retained models, the clearest time-use pattern is a format-specific rating gradient: Stronger players use less time on average in blitz, but more in rapid and especially classical, implying that the relationship between skill and time allocation changes direction across formats. Low-time frequency was found to increase with rating in all formats, especially blitz.




Per table \ref{tab:timeuse-mean-model-comparison} interaction specifications were retained at both levels due to slightly superior WRMSE (0.143 vs. 0.149 for macro and 1.832 vs. 1.839 for player-month). Therefore, the substantive results should be interpreted in terms of format-specific rating relationships rather than one universal rating slope. Notably, blitz is the only of the three with a negative rating gradient, and classical presents a much wider confidence interval, suggesting greater uncertainty (see table \ref{tab:timeuse-player-mean-profile}).




Low-time frequency increases with rating in all three formats. As shown in table \ref{tab:timeuse-lowtime-profile} the absolute level of low-time pressure is highest in blitz, lower in rapid, and lowest in classical. For contrast, the lowest predicted low-time rate in blitz (0.0209 or 2.09% in the 800-rating bin) is greater than the highest predicted low-time rate in classical (0.0194 or 1.94% in the 2400-rating bin). Just as with the mean models, classical estimates are more uncertain than those for blitz and rapid. This means that, even though higher-rated players are more likely to enter low-time states in every format, the baseline prevalence of those states differs sharply across formats.





In blitz, higher-rated players use less time on average but experience more low-time pressure. In rapid and classical, higher-rated players use more time on average but still experience more low-time pressure.
```{r Time-Use Results Figure}
#| label: fig-time-use-results
#| fig-cap: "Predicted time-use values across rating bins."
#| fig-align: center

p_time_panels <- readRDS("Paper_files/figure-rds/p_time_panels.rds")
p_time_panels
```

The size of the format differences is substantial. Blitz remains the fastest format across the rating range, classical the slowest, and rapid falls between them. More importantly, the slope changes sign across formats, which supports treating time control as more than a nuisance adjustment; it changes the way player strength relates to deliberation time. A single common rating effect would have obscured this distinction.

The low-time results tell a different-yet-complementary story. Low-time frequency increases with rating in blitz, rapid, and classical alike. The baseline prevalence of low-time states still differs sharply by format – with blitz much higher than rapid or classical – but within each format, stronger players are predicted to enter low-time situations more often. This is important because it shows that low-time frequency is not merely the inverse of average pace. A player can move faster on average and still enter acute time pressure more often, or spend more time on average and also enter low-time states more often.

These results suggest that time management is multi-dimensional; average pace reflects one aspect of behavior, but low-time exposure reflects another. In blitz, stronger players appear to play faster on average while also entering low-time states more often. In rapid and classical, stronger players spend more time on average yet still show higher low-time frequency. This combination implies that stronger players may be allocating time more selectively rather than simply playing uniformly faster or slower. Additional time-use diagnostics, robustness checks, and predicted profiles are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-d].

### Player Progression {#sec-player-progression-3}
<!--
The retained player fixed-effects models are being used to assess whether within-player changes in current-month behavior are associated with later rating movement, and if so, which behaviors are associated with what kinds of change (i.e., rating gain/loss). Three targets were retained: 1-month rating change, 3-month change, and absolute 1-month change. The signed (non-absolute) targets ask whether a predictor relates to a player moving up or down in rating, with positive values reflecting positive increases and vice versa. In contrast, the absolute target removes direction, and asks whether a predictor relates to moving more or less, regardless of direction—  positive values reflect larger changes, while negative ones imply smaller ones. 
-->

The retained player fixed-effects models relate within-player month-to-month behavior to later rating movement. Across the signed-change targets, the clearest positive predictors of later rating gain are average moves, opening diversity, and switching one’s most-played opening. By contrast, game volume and top-opening concentration show weaker and less consistent evidence.

Table \ref{tab:progression-fe-results} provides the central inferential summary. For both the 1-month and 3-month signed targets, higher current average rating is associated with more negative subsequent signed rating change, while average moves, opening diversity, and switching the most-played opening are positively associated with later change. These effects are directionally consistent across the two signed targets, while games played and top-opening share show weaker and less consistent evidence.

```{=latex}
Top-Opening Share & Absolute 1-Month Change & -5.837 & [-13.635, 1.961] & 0.133 \\
Switched Most-Played Opening & Absolute 1-Month Change & -3.755 & [-4.344, -3.166] & $< 0.001$ \\
\end{xltabular}
```

@fig-player-progression-results makes the main contrast clearer. Average moves, opening diversity, and switching one’s most-played opening are positively associated with later signed rating change, while current rating is negatively associated with it. The negative current-rating coefficient likely reflects both ceiling effects and short-run reversion, leaving the more behaviorally interesting signal in game complexity and repertoire adjustment.

The absolute-change model helps interpret those signed results. None of the favorable signed predictors is positively associated with greater movement magnitude; if anything, average moves, opening diversity, and switching are associated with smaller absolute month-to-month movement. This weakens the interpretation that the signed results are merely artifacts of noisier or more volatile play.

Substantively, the results point toward adaptation and complexity instead of volume alone. Months with longer games, broader repertoires, and a change in the most-played opening are associated with more favorable later signed rating movement, while raw game count is weak and inconclusive once these other behavioral measures are included. These results should still be interpreted as within-player associations, but they consistently suggest that richer and less static opening behavior is more closely linked to later rating gains than sheer activity volume. Additional predictive comparisons, fixed-effects robustness checks, and supplemental results are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-e].

It's important to remember that the fixed-effect design isolates within-player association; these targets are being modeled as within-player associations, not as cross-sectional differences between players. ### Player Categorization {#sec-player-categorization-3}

The retained clustering results are descriptive rather than inferential, so the goal of this subsection is to summarize recurring behavioral profiles rather than to identify definitive player “types.” Even with that caution in place, the retained categorization solution reveals meaningful structure in the player-month data. The clusters differ along several behavioral axes at once, including rating, rating differential, game length, repertoire breadth, opening concentration, and opening switching.

The point here is not to treat the clusters as latent causal types, but to describe recurring patterns in performance, repertoire structure, and activity. Tables \ref{tab:categorization-performance-profiles} and \ref{tab:categorization-repertoire-profiles} summarize the core descriptive profiles. The clusters are not simply a relabeling of average rating. Instead, they combine performance, repertoire, and game-structure features into distinct configurations. Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 form a particularly clear contrast: Cluster 1 is associated with a broader repertoire, higher rating, and longer games, whereas Cluster 2 is narrower, lower rated, and associated with shorter games. Cluster 3 is especially notable for very high switching, while Cluster 6 is more concentrated and stable in its opening behavior. Clusters 4 and 5 both include relatively stronger players, but differ in the kind of behavioral profile they summarize. Collectively, these contrasts suggest that the retained solution is capturing multiple styles of engagement.

The cluster distributions also vary by time control. Some profiles are more common in blitz, while others appear more often in classical, with rapid tending to be more evenly distributed. These differences should not be over-read, especially where classical support is thinner, but they do suggest that format is part of the behavioral structure the clustering solution is capturing. The profiles are therefore not purely abstract player labels; they are partly shaped by the time-control context in which behavior is observed.

@fig-cluster-heatmap helps clarify how these profiles should be interpreted over time. Some clusters show substantial persistence from one month to the next, but switching is also common, and the transition structure is clearly patterned. This is the key reason the clusters are better understood as recurring behavioral states. They capture meaningful structure in player behavior, but that structure appears fluid enough that many players move among states over time instead of remaining locked into a single class.

This state-based interpretation is consistent with the rest of the paper’s results. The opening ecosystem broadens over time, opening choice varies with strength and format, time use is multi-dimensional, and progression is associated with adaptation. Against that background, recurring-but-fluid behavioral states are a more plausible interpretation than sharply-bounded and permanent classes. Additional clustering specification details, time-control composition summaries, persistence summaries, and robustness diagnostics are reported in Appendix [-@sec-appendix-f].

### Principal Findings {#sec-discussion}

The retained models point to structured variation in online chess behavior across both ecosystem-level and player-level domains. At the ecosystem level, the metagame became less concentrated and more diverse over time. At the opening-choice level, popularity varied systematically by rating and time control. In the time-use domain, average pacing and low-time frequency behaved as related but distinct dimensions of player behavior. In the progression models, favorable later rating movement was associated more consistently with game complexity, repertoire breadth, and repertoire adjustment than with raw activity volume. Finally, the clustering results suggested that player behavior is better summarized as a set of recurring behavioral profiles than as a small number of fixed player types.

In aggregate, these findings argue against simple, one-dimensional explanations. Metagame change was not primarily a story of one opening taking over. Time management was not reducible to a single measure of efficiency. Progression was not best explained by game volume alone. Instead, the results repeatedly point toward diversification, conditional behavior, and adaptation. The subsections that follow interpret those patterns in greater depth and consider what they imply about metagame change, player decision-making, development, and the broader study of online chess behavior.

The main interpretive question, then, is not whether structure exists, but what the structure suggests about metagame change, player decision-making, and behavioral development.

One of the most consistent patterns present in the results is that they repeatedly argue against simple, one-dimensional explanations: metagame change was not just a story of one opening taking over, time management was not reducible to one general measure of efficiency, and progression was not best explained by activity volume alone. Instead, the findings point toward more diverse outcomes. Diversification is interesting because a simple prior expectation might have been convergence around a smaller number of dominant openings or strategies; it suggests that greater access to theory, engines, and content may be expanding participation in the opening space rather than narrowing it, and implies that player development may benefit more from experimentation and differentiation than optimization towards one best repertoire.

The subsections that follow interpret these findings in greater depth, focusing on what they imply about metagame evolution, opening choice, time-management behavior, progression, and the meaning of the retained behavioral profiles.^[Though no prior expectations were formally established at this project's outset, the subsections may sometimes draw comparisons between the results and hypothetical expectations which might otherwise have been made.]

-->

### Metagame Structure and Opening Choice {#sec-metagame-and-opening-discussion}

The strongest ecosystem-level finding was the paired decline in concentration and rise in effective diversity across time controls. In substantive terms, the metagame broadened over the study period. That result matters because a common expectation in competitive environments is some degree of convergence toward a relatively narrow set of dominant strategies, especially when players have broad access to shared theory, engine analysis, and educational content. The present results instead suggest a more expansive pattern, in which opening use became less concentrated rather than more so.

That conclusion should still be interpreted cautiously. Our results do not identify the mechanism behind this broadening, nor can they determine whether the same pattern would appear on other platforms or in other eras of online chess. Even so, the outcome is notable. One plausible interpretation is that large online player populations support a wider range of viable strategic habits than a narrower or more homogeneous competitive environment would. Another is simply that chess is strategically rich enough that increased access to information does not mechanically force population behavior into a small set of dominant lines.

The opening-popularity results sharpen that picture. Opening choice varied much more clearly by rating and time control than by calendar time. Stronger players allocated less share to the most common named openings and more to the residual “Other” category, while time control modified that structure rather than replacing it. Temporal movement was directionally consistent with the broader metagame results, but comparatively modest in magnitude. The opening landscape therefore looks less like a rapidly-rotating cycle of named openings and more like a layered system of skill-stratified preferences with gradual long-run drift.

It is also useful to distinguish between two kinds of diversification. One possibility would be simple turnover among the same small set of highly popular openings. The other, which is more consistent with the present results, is a broader expansion in the share allocated outside that narrow top set. The latter interpretation is more substantively important, because it suggests widening participation in the opening space rather than mere reshuffling among a fixed group of choices.

Overall, these results support a picture of gradual diversification rather than convergence, with broadening driven more by long-tail expansion and skill-stratified choice than by visible turnover among a small set of named openings.

While the results cannot support an inferential claim about whether the increase in diversity is a result of an online chess environment compared to chess itself, it isn't implausible to speculate that the massive quantity of diverse people playing online chess may be fostering diversification by pushing back against a strategic collapse toward a few dominant lines. On the opening-choice front, the clearest structure in opening popularity came from rating and format rather than over-time drift. The results found that opening choice was deeply stratified by player strength, with time control modifying the player-strength structure instead of replacing it. Temporal changes are directionally consistent across formats, but modest in magnitude. The opening metagame therefore looks like a layered system of skill-stratified preferences plus moderate temporal drift.

Important is the distinction between diversification as a measure of which openings are most popular and diversification as a measure of total opening share. The former implies that the top openings simply shuffled around, cyclically taking each other's place over time, while the latter implies that the share of the Other category of openings actually increases over time. This dichotomy is important because metagames often move in cyclical patterns, best illustrated by the game of rock-paper-scissors.

Suppose that chess openings can be likened to rock-paper-scissors, where any given opening can map to one of the three options— rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. Now suppose that 50% of chess players favor openings which map to rock, while scissors and paper are each only favored by 25% of players. Assuming completely random matchmaking, scissors-style openings become disproportionately likely to lose, and paper-style openings become conversely likely to win. Canny players will recognize this dynamic, and begin to play paper at a higher rate. Let's say 15% of all scissors players switch to paper. Now, scissors has the disproportionate advantage. That is, until rock players catch on and swap to paper and the cycle repeats itself. In a perfect world, the metagame would converge to a point where each type had an opening share of $1/3$, but in practice, metagames tend to remain cyclical.

Now, it isn't actually reasonable to map chess openings to a rock-paper-scissors structure, but that's not the point of the hypothetical. The point is that even after converging to a point where rock, paper, and scissors each have an equal opening share, there are still only three options in use; if the top openings shift around, but the quantity of unique openings played remains the same, then all that's really happened is a shift among the most popular openings. The opening diversification supported by the results contrast such an eventuality by showing that the Other category of openings is actually increasing in share over time, which suggests that the Lichess playerbase is expanding in breadth.

Overall, these findings complicate at least two simple expectations: First, more theory and shared content might have led to convergence, and second, metagame change might have been expected to appear mostly as visible named-opening turnover. Instead, the results suggest broad diversification, long-tail expansion, and strong rating structuring.

### Time Management as Multi-Dimensional Behavior {#sec-time-discussion}

The time-use results suggest that time management is not a one-dimensional behavioral trait. Average time use and low-time frequency are related, but they capture different aspects of play. Across formats, the relationship between rating and average time use changed sign: Stronger players moved faster on average in blitz, but used more time on average in rapid and classical. At the same time, low-time frequency increased with rating in every format.

This matters because it changes the way time use should be interpreted. In blitz, faster average play among stronger players may reflect greater fluency, pattern recognition, or reliance on stable priors. In slower formats, greater average time use may instead reflect deeper calculation, more deliberate planning, or a higher willingness to invest time in critical positions. The same amount of time spent per move therefore does not have the same meaning across formats. Time control is not merely a nuisance adjustment; it changes the behavioral interpretation of pacing itself.

The low-time results reinforce that point. A simple expectation might be that stronger players use time more smoothly and therefore avoid acute time pressure. The retained models suggest otherwise. Stronger players were more likely to enter low-time states in blitz, rapid, and classical alike. This does not imply poor time management. Rather, it suggests that stronger players may allocate time more selectively, accepting later pressure in exchange for deeper thinking when they judge it worthwhile.

Together, these findings support a view of time management as multi-dimensional. Baseline pace and acute time-pressure exposure are not interchangeable, and neither can be reduced to a single global measure of “better” or “worse” time use. More broadly, the results suggest that time management is itself a meaningful behavioral domain rather than merely a mechanical byproduct of format.

### Progression, Adaptation, and Player Development {#sec-player-progression-discussion}

A simple expectation about skill development is that more practice should lead to more improvement. In the context of online chess, that expectation would imply that raw activity volume is the strongest predictor of subsequent rating gains. The retained progression models did not support that view. Instead, more favorable later rating movement was associated more consistently with longer games, greater opening diversity, and switching the most-played opening. By contrast, games played was comparatively weak and inconclusive once these other behavioral measures were included.

This pattern suggests that player development may depend more on the character of engagement than on volume alone. Broader repertoires and changes in the most-played opening are consistent with adaptation, experimentation, or strategic flexibility. Longer games may likewise reflect more complex or demanding play. None of these interpretations can be treated as causal, but together they support a developmental account in which richer engagement matters more than repetition by itself.

The absolute-change model further clarifies the signed-change results. The predictors associated with favorable signed rating movement were not associated with larger absolute swings. If anything, average moves, opening diversity, and switching were associated with smaller absolute month-to-month movement. That pattern weakens the interpretation that the signed results are merely artifacts of noisier or more volatile play. The progression findings therefore do not look like a story of high-risk experimentation producing bigger swings in either direction. They look more like a story of gradual improvement associated with adaptation and complexity.

This does not mean that playing more games is irrelevant. A more careful interpretation is that raw volume has limited additional explanatory value once more behaviorally informative measures are taken into account. In that sense, the retained models suggest diminishing returns to volume alone and a stronger role for adaptive engagement. Improvement, at least in this setting, appears better characterized as an adaptive process than as a purely cumulative one.

### Behavioral Profiles as Descriptive States {#sec-categorization-discussion}

The clustering results are best interpreted descriptively. They do not justify strong inferential claims about latent player “types,” but they do indicate that player-month observations contain enough structure to be grouped into recurring behavioral profiles. Those profiles vary along multiple axes at once, including skill, repertoire breadth, opening concentration, switching behavior, game length, and outcome structure. That is important because it means the clustering solution is not merely reproducing the platform’s rating hierarchy under a different name.

The retained profiles are most naturally interpreted as states rather than fixed identities. Some persistence is clearly present, but so are patterned transitions between clusters. Players do not appear to remain locked into a single behavioral class over time. Instead, the evidence suggests movement among recurring configurations of behavior. That reading is consistent with the rest of the paper’s findings: The opening environment broadens over time, time use depends on context, and progression is associated with adaptation rather than rigidity. Against that background, recurring-but-fluid behavioral states are a more plausible interpretation than sharply-bounded and permanent player types.

This interpretation also helps explain why the clustering results are useful despite their inferential limits. Their value does not come from proving the existence of a small number of true latent player categories. It comes from showing that player behavior is structured enough to support interpretable recurring profiles. That in turn suggests a promising direction for later work— modeling movement among behavioral states directly.

The clustering models are in somewhat of a tricky spot, because even though they were largely successful, they're unfit for inference. As such, this section makes no attempts to provide conclusive or inferential claims, and instead intends to ask what it means for the clustering to have succeeded and the potential implications of that success.

The retained clustering solution differentiates player-month among multiple behavioral axes: skill, repertoire breadth, opening switching, game length and draw structure, and activity. For example, cluster 1 contains high-diversity, high-activity, and above-average-rated players, while cluster 2 contrasts this with, with lower-rated, low-activity, narrower-repertoire players. This is salient because it means the model isn't simply reproducing the Lichess skill ranking, and instead identifies distinct configurations of chess behavior.

Were the clusters sharply stable, they might look like enduring player types, but because persistence is moderate and transitions between clusters are common, they're better interpreted as recurring behavioral states or configurations. This descriptive-state reading is consistent with the rest of the results: A broadening opening ecosystem and adaptive progression patterns both suggest behavioral movement, so the clusters may therefore reflect temporary strategic priorities, developmental phases, or context-dependent styles. This makes them useful as summaries of behavior, but not as definitive labels of what a player 'is'.

Ultimately, although the retained clustering solution is not itself inferential, its success suggest that player behavior is structured enough to motivate more explicit state-based analyses in future work. Because the clusters are both interpretable and fluid, a natural next step would be to model transitions among behavioral profiles directly and ask how those movements relate to development, format, or repertoire change. In short, the fact that the models work so well at classifying player behavior is more important than any of their descriptive interpretations.
-->

### Practical Uses and Broader Implications {#sec-implications-discussion}

Methodologically, the project shows that linked models of metagame structure, opening choice, time use, progression, and behavioral profiling can be integrated within a single analytic framework. These domains are often studied separately, but the present results suggest that they are better understood as linked parts of a broader behavioral system.

The results also point to possible practical uses in coaching or player-development settings. The progression models suggest that broader and more adaptive engagement may be more informative than game volume alone. The time-use results suggest that average pace and low-time pressure should be treated as distinct aspects of behavior rather than collapsed into one summary metric. Together, these findings imply that player-facing tools may be more useful when they track repertoire breadth, adjustment, and time-use patterns alongside more familiar performance measures.

More broadly, the paper shows that large-scale online game logs can support behavioral analysis without reducing chess to engine evaluation alone. Chess is especially well suited to this kind of work because it combines standardized rules, rich decision structure, repeated play, and a mature rating system. As a result, it offers a useful environment for studying adaptation, strategic diversity, and development in a naturally occurring competitive setting.

### Limitations {#sec-limitations-discussion}

The most important limitation of the project is that it is observational throughout. The results support associations, not causal claims. For example, opening diversity and repertoire adjustment are associated with more favorable later rating movement, but the models do not establish that increasing diversity or switching openings causes improvement. Likewise, the time-use results describe behavioral signatures associated with skill and format, not causal mechanisms of stronger play. Even the fixed-effects models, while stronger than purely cross-sectional comparisons, do not eliminate time-varying confounding.

A second limitation concerns data scope and analytic breadth. The project was intentionally designed to be reproducible and to address several substantive questions within one framework. That choice made the analysis broader, but it also constrained how deeply any one domain could be modeled. A more specialized study could devote more of the sample, feature design, and model structure to a single problem, such as move-level decision quality, richer opening taxonomy, or transition dynamics among behavioral profiles.

The models also compress a strategically complex environment into tractable summaries. That compression is unavoidable. Chess is too rich to model exhaustively at scale, so each analytic task relies on reduced representations of a much more detailed behavioral space. Some simplifications are especially visible in the opening models, which rely on a top-$k$ structure with a substantively meaningful but still heterogeneous “Other” category, and in the use of relatively simple functional forms in several retained models. These choices are reasonable for the present project, but they still limit how finely the results can characterize behavior.

Finally, the findings are specific to the Lichess platform and to the January 2024 through December 2025 study window. They should therefore be interpreted as results about that setting, not as definitive descriptions of online chess as a whole. Other platforms, populations, or periods may display similar patterns, but they may also differ in meaningful ways.

All inference presented in this work is therefore limited to associations between variables rather than claims that one directly influences the other. For example, opening diversity and switching are associated with rating increase, but the models do not prove that increasing diversity or switching causes improvement; similarly, time-use patterns should not be read as causal mechanisms of strength and instead as correlated behavioral signatures. Even the fixed-effects models, while stronger than purely cross-sectional comparisons, still do not eliminate all time-varying confounding. This is the project's most important limitation: That all retained results are derived from observational data, so even the strongest inferential findings must be interpreted as such.

Second, the data gathered for the project was intentionally limited in size and scope— size for reproducibility purposes, and scope because the project set out to explore several facets of online chess behavior. In a more focused study, the modeling process would have access to a dataset tailored to the project's specific goals (e.g., the inclusion of move data to better model individual games). Greater specificity can also indirectly afford larger datasets, as those built to accommodate multiple different modeling goals effectively 'waste' space by including fields that aren't necessary for all research questions. Admittedly, this is not a limitation of the core modeling framework so much as a consequence of the format this project was built upon and the concern for reproducibility therein, but the reason for a limitations existence does not obviate its effect.

Also related to the scope and scale of the data is granularity. The game of chess is an unfathomably-complex strategic space, to the point that it's functionally impossible to model in full detail; there is simply not a computer on the planet that could even get close to accomplishing such a task. To that end, each model necessarily compresses a much richer behavioral space into something capable of being modeled. Part of this compression happened during the parsing pipeline (see @sec-source), but some models took additional steps to further simplify the data. For instance, the top-$k$ opening models rely on a large residual Other category, which is substantively meaningful but still aggregates many heterogeneous openings; some retained models depend on linear or otherwise simple functional forms; and some estimates, especially in slower formats or sparse settings, are less stable or more uncertain.

Finally, it must be acknowledged that the data used for modeling are both relative to a specific platform in Lichess and dependent on the time period studied. The results should accordingly not be used to describe online chess behavior as a whole, but interpreted in the context of the Lichess population from January 2024 through December 2025. It might be that other platforms like Chess.com show similar results or that the Lichess ecosystem behaved very similarly in years prior to 2024, but it's equally possible that those alternate populations behave in entirely different manners.

### Future Work {#sec-future-work}

A natural next step is to apply the retained framework more deeply within specific domains. Especially promising directions include move-level decision-quality analysis, richer opening annotation, longer player histories, and explicit modeling of transitions among behavioral profiles. These extensions would preserve the present paper’s core structure while allowing much deeper treatment of individual behavioral domains.

Several specific empirical questions also follow directly from the present results. One is whether metagame broadening reflects genuine experimentation or primarily long-tail expansion in opening choice. Another is whether the higher low-time frequency observed among stronger players reflects sharper positions, more selective time investment, or some other feature of high-level play. A third is whether repertoire adjustment is a precursor to improvement or merely one correlate of broader behavioral change. These questions are not fully answerable within the current design, but they are clearly motivated by the retained findings.

A final priority is external validation. Because the results are tied to one platform and one time window, cross-platform and cross-period replication would be especially valuable. Replication on other platforms, or on earlier and later Lichess periods, would help distinguish patterns that are specific to this environment from those that are more general features of online chess. If the framework proves stable across settings, it could support a broader comparative research program on strategic behavior and skill development in competitive online environments.

```{=latex}
\texttt{player} & categorical & Deterministic pseudonymous user ID (e.g., \texttt{u\us ...}). Identifies a player across months in longitudinal summaries. \\
\texttt{month} & categorical & Month of play as \texttt{YYYY-MM}. Primary time index for longitudinal analysis. \\
\texttt{games} & numeric (count) & Number of games played by the player in the month. Also a reliability/weighting signal. \\
\texttt{wins} & numeric (count) & Count of wins in the month. \\
\texttt{losses} & numeric (count) & Count of losses in the month. \\
\texttt{draws} & numeric (count) & Count of draws in the month. \\
\texttt{win\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Wins divided by games. Primary performance measure in player-level models. \\
\texttt{draw\us rate} & numeric (proportion) & Draws divided by games. Useful because draw propensity varies by skill and style. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating} & numeric & Average of the player’s pre-game rating across games in the month. Primary skill proxy. \\
\texttt{avg\us opp\us rating} & numeric & Average opponent pre-game rating in the month. Contextualizes performance and approximates strength of schedule. \\
\texttt{avg\us rating\us diff} & numeric & Average (player rating minus opponent rating) across games in the month. Summarizes typical matchup difficulty. \\
\texttt{avg\us moves} & numeric & Average game length in moves. Proxy for style and game complexity. \\
\texttt{opening\us diversity} & numeric (count) & Number of distinct openings used in the month. Proxy for repertoire breadth. \\
\texttt{top\us opening} & categorical & Most frequently played opening during the month (ties broken deterministically). Summary of dominant repertoire choice. \\
\end{xltabular}
```

## Exploratory Diagnostics and Support {#sec-appendix-b}

### Reliability

```{r Reliability Plot}
#| label: fig-reliability
#| fig-cap: "Player-month observations have highly unequal reliability. The dataset has a long, right-skewed tail of heavy-activity players, which risk dominating aggregates if not uncontrolled for."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

gdist <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT games
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE games <= 250
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(gdist, aes(x=games)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 250)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Games per Player in a Given Month", y = "Rows", title = "Player-Month Reliability Varies Widely") +
  theme_few()
```

```{r Coverage-by-Rating Plot}
#| label: fig-coverage-rating
#| fig-cap: "Player-month observations have highly unequal reliability. The dataset has a long, right-skewed tail of heavy-activity players, which risk dominating aggregates if not uncontrolled for."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

bin_width <- 200

support_by_rating2 <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating / %d) * %d AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin,
    COUNT(*) AS n_rows,
    SUM(games) AS total_games
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE avg_rating IS NOT NULL
    AND games IS NOT NULL
    AND tc_bucket IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", bin_width, bin_width, qpath(paths$pm_tc))) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(n_rows, total_games),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "support"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      n_rows = "Row Count",
      total_games = "Summed Games"
    ),
    tc_bucket = factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical"))
  )

ggplot(support_by_rating2, aes(x = rating_bin, y = support)) +
  geom_col(width = bin_width * 0.9, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  facet_grid(
    measure ~ tc_bucket,
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = labeller(
      tc_bucket = c(blitz = "Blitz", rapid = "Rapid", classical = "Classical")
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks(n = 7)) +
  labs(
    x = "Rating Bin",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Support Across Rating Bins by Time Control",
    subtitle = "Compares POM_TC Row Counts with Summed Games"
  ) +
  theme_few() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

### Rating-Change Noise Diagnostics

```{r Rating Changes Plot}
#| label: fig-delta-rating
#| fig-cap: "Rating change is centered near zero with roughly symmetric dispersion. Most month-to-month changes are small, so effect sizes will likely be modest."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

chg <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, month, avg_rating
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
  ),
  y AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      avg_rating,
      LAG(avg_rating) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS prev_rating
    FROM x
  )
  SELECT (avg_rating - prev_rating) AS d_rating
  FROM y
  WHERE prev_rating IS NOT NULL AND d_rating >= -300 AND d_rating <= 300
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(chg, aes(x=d_rating)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=80, fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Month-to-Month Change in Average Rating", y = "Count", 
       title = "Distribution of Within-Player Rating Change") +
  theme_few()
```

```{r Volatility Plot}
#| label: fig-volatility
#| fig-cap: "Observed rating movement behaves like a measurement-error problem; the number of games played is inversely proportional to rating-change volatility. This is expected behavior for a rating system."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

vol <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, month, games, avg_rating
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
  ),
  y AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      games,
      avg_rating,
      LAG(avg_rating) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS prev_rating
    FROM x
  )
  SELECT
    games,
    ABS(avg_rating - prev_rating) AS abs_d_rating
  FROM y
  WHERE prev_rating IS NOT NULL
", qpath(paths$pm)))

ggplot(vol, aes(x = games, y = abs_d_rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") +
  labs(x = "Games per Month (Log-Transformed)", y = "Absolute Change in Rating (|Δ|)",
       title = "Monthly Rating Volatility Shrinks as Game Volume Rises",
       subtitle = "Log-Transformed for Legibility") +
  theme_few()
```

### Time-Pressure Diagnostics

```{r LTD}
#| label: fig-low-time-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Lorem ipsum."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

min_moves_ptm <- 40
positive_binwidth <- 0.01

ltr_dist <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    low_time_rate,
    move_rows
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  WHERE tc_bucket IS NOT NULL
    AND low_time_rate IS NOT NULL
    AND move_rows IS NOT NULL
    AND move_rows >= %d
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc), min_moves_ptm))

zero_panel <- ltr_dist %>%
  mutate(panel = "Zero mass", x_cat = if_else(low_time_rate == 0, "0%", ">0%")) %>%
  count(tc_bucket, panel, x_cat, name = "n")

positive_panel <- ltr_dist %>%
  filter(low_time_rate > 0) %>%
  mutate(panel = "Positive support")

p1 <- ggplot(zero_panel, aes(x = x_cat, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(
    ~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")),
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rows",
    title = "Exact Zero Mass"
  ) +
  theme_few()

p2 <- ggplot(positive_panel, aes(x = low_time_rate)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = positive_binwidth,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")),
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Low-Time Rate",
    y = "Rows",
    title = "Low-Time Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_few()

p2 / p1
```

```{r LTR}
#| label: fig-low-time
#| fig-cap: "Low-time rate is zero-inflated and noisy. Time-control-specific curves are underpowered (with the exception of blitz), and pooling is needed for stable inference. Any relationship between time trouble and improvement is likely both small and nonlinear, which is why loess smoothing wasn't applied to this figure."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

min_games_pm   <- 5     # require at least this many games in the month (across all TCs)
min_moves_ptm  <- 25    # require at least this many move rows in the month (across all TCs)

ltr_scatter_all <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH pm_tc AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      avg_rating,
      games
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE player IS NOT NULL
      AND month  IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
  ),
  pm AS (
    -- collapse across time controls using games-weighted avg_rating
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      SUM(games) AS games_total,
      SUM(avg_rating * games) / SUM(games) AS avg_rating_all
    FROM pm_tc
    GROUP BY player, month
    HAVING SUM(games) >= %d
  ),
  pm_next AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      games_total,
      avg_rating_all,
      LEAD(avg_rating_all) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS next_rating_all
    FROM pm
  ),
  delta AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      games_total,
      avg_rating_all,
      (next_rating_all - avg_rating_all) AS d_rating_next
    FROM pm_next
    WHERE next_rating_all IS NOT NULL
  ),
  ptm_tc AS (
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      low_time_rate,
      move_rows
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE player IS NOT NULL
      AND month  IS NOT NULL
      AND low_time_rate IS NOT NULL
      AND move_rows IS NOT NULL
  ),
  ptm AS (
    -- collapse across time controls using move_rows-weighted low_time_rate
    SELECT
      player,
      month,
      SUM(move_rows) AS move_rows_total,
      SUM(low_time_rate * move_rows) / SUM(move_rows) AS low_time_rate_all
    FROM ptm_tc
    GROUP BY player, month
    HAVING SUM(move_rows) >= %d
  )
  SELECT
    d.player,
    d.month,
    d.avg_rating_all,
    d.games_total,
    d.d_rating_next,
    p.low_time_rate_all,
    p.move_rows_total
  FROM delta d
  JOIN ptm p USING (player, month)
", qpath(paths$pm_tc), min_games_pm,
   qpath(paths$ptm_tc), min_moves_ptm))

ggplot(ltr_scatter_all, aes(x = low_time_rate_all, y = d_rating_next)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  ylim(-225, 225) +
  labs(
    x = "Low-Time Rate",
    y = "Next-Month Δ Rating",
    title = "Time Trouble vs Next-Month Rating Change",
    subtitle = "Collapsed Across Time Controls"
  ) +
  theme_few()
```

### Supplemental Exploratory Plots by Topic

```{r Opening Trends Helper}
plot_opening_trends <- function(tc_use, fig_title) {
  top_openings <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
    WITH x AS (
      SELECT opening, SUM(games) AS total_games
      FROM read_parquet(%s)
      WHERE tc_bucket='%s' AND opening IS NOT NULL
      GROUP BY opening
    )
    SELECT opening
    FROM x
    ORDER BY total_games DESC
    LIMIT 8
  ", qpath(paths$mom_tc), tc_use))

  open_list <- paste0("('", paste(gsub("'", "''", top_openings$opening), collapse="','"), "')")

  trend <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
    WITH filtered AS (
      SELECT month, tc_bucket, opening, games
      FROM read_parquet(%s)
      WHERE tc_bucket='%s'
        AND opening IN %s
        AND opening IS NOT NULL
    ),
    opening_level AS (
      SELECT
        month,
        tc_bucket,
        opening,
        SUM(games) AS games
      FROM filtered
      GROUP BY month, tc_bucket, opening
    )
    SELECT
      month,
      tc_bucket,
      opening,
      games,
      CAST(games AS DOUBLE) / SUM(games) OVER (PARTITION BY month, tc_bucket) AS share
    FROM opening_level
    ORDER BY month, opening
  ", qpath(paths$mom_tc), tc_use, open_list))

  ggplot(trend, aes(x = month, y = share, color = opening, group = opening)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
    labs(
      x = "Month",
      y = "Share of Games",
      color = "",
      title = fig_title,
      subtitle = "Top Eight Openings in Terms of Game Share"
    ) +
    scale_color_few() +
    theme_few() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1)
    ) +
    guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE))
}
```

```{r Allocation Profile by Rating}
#| label: fig-time-allocation
#| fig-cap: "All three time controls have distinct time-usage patterns when game phases are additionally factored in."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H

phase <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  SELECT
    tc_bucket,
    FLOOR(avg_rating/200)*200 AS rating_bin,
    AVG(avg_time_opening) AS t_open,
    AVG(avg_time_middlegame) AS t_mid,
    AVG(avg_time_endgame) AS t_end,
    SUM(move_rows) AS total_moves
  FROM read_parquet(%s)
  GROUP BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
  HAVING total_moves >= 10000
  ORDER BY tc_bucket, rating_bin
", qpath(paths$ptm_tc)))

phase_long <- phase |>
  pivot_longer(cols=c(t_open, t_mid, t_end),
                      names_to="phase", values_to="sec")

ggplot(phase_long, aes(x=rating_bin, y=sec, color=phase, group=phase)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~factor(tc_bucket, levels = c("blitz", "rapid", "classical")), scales="free_y", labeller = as_labeller(c(
      blitz = "Blitz",
      rapid = "Rapid",
      classical = "Classical"
    ))) +
  labs(x="Rating", y="Seconds per Move", color = "Phase",
       title="Phase Time Allocation by Rating") +
  scale_color_few(labels = c("Endgame", "Middlegame", "Opening")) +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

```

```{r Div Strata}
#| label: fig-strata
#| fig-cap: "Line color indicates number of games played, while the x-axis show the number of unique openings a player used within a given month."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-pos: H
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8

div_strata <- dbGetQuery(con, sprintf("
  WITH x AS (
    SELECT player, month, opening_diversity, games, avg_rating
    FROM read_parquet(%s)
    WHERE opening_diversity IS NOT NULL
      AND games IS NOT NULL
      AND avg_rating IS NOT NULL
  ),
  y AS (
    SELECT *,
      LEAD(avg_rating) OVER (PARTITION BY player ORDER BY month) AS next_rating
    FROM x
  ),
  z AS (
    SELECT
      CAST(FLOOR(avg_rating/200)*200 AS INTEGER) AS rating_bin,
      CASE
        WHEN games < 10 THEN '<10'
        WHEN games < 25 THEN '10–24'
        WHEN games < 60 THEN '25–59'
        ELSE '60+'
      END AS games_bin,
      opening_diversity,
      (next_rating - avg_rating) AS d_rating_next
    FROM y
    WHERE next_rating IS NOT NULL
  )
  SELECT
    rating_bin,
    games_bin,
    opening_diversity,
    AVG(d_rating_next) AS mean_d,
    COUNT(*) AS n
  FROM z
  GROUP BY rating_bin, games_bin, opening_diversity
  HAVING n >= 5
  ORDER BY rating_bin, games_bin, opening_diversity
", qpath(paths$pm)))

div_strata <- div_strata |>
  mutate(games_bin = factor(games_bin, levels = c("60+", "25–59", "10–24", "<10")))

ggplot(div_strata, aes(x=opening_diversity, y=mean_d, color=games_bin)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~rating_bin, scales="free_y") +
  labs(x="Opening Diversity (Within-Month)", y="Mean Next-Month Δ Rating",
       color="Games",
       title="Opening Diversity vs Improvement",
       subtitle = "Stratified by Games and Rating") +
  scale_color_few() +
  theme_few() + 
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

```
